CLASS 38 · AGES 4–5 · 35 FEELINGS & KINDNESS LESSONS

Feelings & Kindness.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Thirty-five cards, four words each, one kinder vocabulary.

Every card in this class teaches four words a four-year-old actually needs: the feeling faces (happy, sad, angry, calm — then the bigger ones), the kind habits (share, help, take turns, include), the calm-down skills (breathe, pause, count to ten, reset) and the belonging words (you matter, I am here, we care). Each card opens its own step-by-step lesson — what the words mean, the three ideas your child needs, the parent script, one game for the living room and the moment in your real day where the words already live. The order is deliberate: feelings first, kindness second, the tricky words honestly in the middle, and the choice at the end.

One card a sitting is plenty — the whole class is a term of five-minute feelings talks. The vocabulary is the one early-years teachers use in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand: social-emotional learning, emotion vocabulary, feelings check-ins and calm-down skills — the same words preschools teach as the heart of the early curriculum. By the last card, your child holds a whole vocabulary for the weather inside — and the standing rule that kindness is a choice, freely made, every time.

WHY FEELINGS FIRST

A feeling with a name is a feeling with a door.

The research keeps landing in the same place: children who can name their feelings need fewer meltdowns to say the same thing, recover faster when the storm lands and ask for help sooner. This class does not train happiness — every feeling on these cards is allowed, from lonely to jealous to embarrassed. It hands your child the words for ALL of them, plus the calm-down skills that make the big ones survivable and the kindness habits that make other people glad your child came.

And the class keeps its place in the Learning Path honestly: it grew out of Class 32 (Life Skills & Good Habits) — the habits shelf — and it is the older cousin of the first feeling faces your child met in the toddler years. Class 32 points here as its next step; the age-two Emotions & Feelings class remains the gentle way in for younger siblings.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Happy, Sad, Angry & Calm — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson opens the whole class the way every feelings teacher does: with the four faces your child already makes every day, and the words that go with them.

What is this?

Happy, sad, angry and calm are the four first feelings — the ones every child meets before they can tie a shoe. Each has its own face, its own body and its own speed: happy spreads, sad droops, angry flashes hot, calm slows everything down.

What does it mean?

For a small child, feelings arrive as weather — big, real and unexplained. Naming them is the first act of social-emotional learning: a feeling with a name becomes something to talk about instead of something that just happens to you.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: every feeling has a FACE (smiles, frowns, eyebrows, soft eyes); every feeling has a BODY (bouncy, droopy, hot, still); and every feeling is allowed — even angry — as long as hands stay kind.

Why this matters

These four words are the load-bearing walls of the whole class: every later card — the tricky ones, the calm-down skills, the kindness words — stands on the ability to say happy, sad, angry or calm and mean it.

What it teaches

Emotion vocabulary (the foundation of self-regulation), face-reading (the first empathy skill), body awareness, and the naming habit that turns feelings into words instead of meltdowns.

Words to learn

happysadangrycalmfeelingfacecalm down

Say this to your child

“"Everybody has feelings — happy days, sad days, angry moments and calm ones, and grown-ups have all four too. Happy is a smile that wants to spread. Sad is when something is gone or wrong. Angry is the hot one — it shows in the eyebrows! And calm is the slow, soft one we can find on purpose with a big breath. All four are allowed. All four have names. And naming them is your superpower."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four feelings live on this card — let us meet them."
  2. Name each face slowly: happy smiles, sad droops, angry shows its eyebrows, calm closes its eyes. Let your child copy each face in a small mirror or at your face.
  3. Play feelings charades: you make one of the four faces, your child names it and makes it back. Swap roles.
  4. Do the body check: "Where does happy live in your body? Where does angry live?" No wrong answers — chests and tummies are common.
  5. Finish with the calm breath below and the takeaway: "Every feeling is okay — and calm is the one we can visit on purpose."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels each show one labeled feeling face: Happy, a boy with a big open smile; Sad, a boy with a downturned mouth; Angry, a boy with furrowed brows; and Calm, a boy with closed eyes and a soft smile — the four faces exactly as they arrive on a small person.

Ask your child

"Which face is the smiley one?" "What does angry look like — show me the eyebrows!" "Which feeling closes its eyes?" "Which one do you feel right now?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Angry has angry eyebrows!" "Calm is the sleeping one" or the proud one: "I am happy RIGHT NOW."

Out in the real world

Feelings live everywhere once you hunt them: characters in books (find the angry face!), people at the bus stop, the dog’s wagging tail-happy and the cat’s annoyed-flat ears. One "look, that man looks calm" on a walk is worth a worksheet.

Try it together

Four-Corners Feelings: label the room’s corners happy, sad, angry, calm. You call a tiny story — "we got ice cream!" "the tower fell!" — and your child runs to the matching corner, making the face on arrival. Five stories, four corners, one giggling vocabulary lesson.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which feeling has angry eyebrows? Which one closes its eyes? Are all four feelings allowed?" Angry, calm, yes — three answers and the first lesson of the class is won.

Parent tips

If angry becomes the only interesting face, lean into calm instead — make it the mysterious, cozy one: "calm is the feeling cats know best." And never rush the body check: children who know WHERE a feeling lives can spot it arriving earlier next time.

This lesson pairs with the Happy, Sad, Angry & Calm flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Kind, Share, Help & Thank You — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns four abstract words into four things your child can DO before lunch — because at four, kindness is a verb, not a poster.

What is this?

Kind, share, help and thank you are the first four kindness words: kind is the friendly heart everything else grows from, share lets someone use what is yours, help lends a hand to someone who needs it and thank you says "I saw what you did."

What does it mean?

Kindness words teach children that their actions have weather — they change how other people feel. That discovery ("I made her happy!") is the seed every later social skill grows from.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: kind is a HEART first (you notice people); share and help are HANDS (they do things); thank you is a MOUTH that closes the circle by naming the kindness out loud.

Why this matters

These four arrive second on the card path because they are the words a child can use within the hour — breakfast offers a share, socks offer a helper, and every gift offers a thank you. Early wins build the kindness habit.

What it teaches

Pro-social behaviour (the psychology name for kindness in action), generosity, perspective-taking beginnings, gratitude practice and the warmth of being caught doing good.

Words to learn

kindsharehelpthank youkind wordsgivefriendly

Say this to your child

“"Kind is the warmest word there is. It means your heart is friendly and your eyes are open — you NOTICE when someone needs something. Share means letting someone in on what is yours. Help means lending your hands to someone whose hands are full. And thank you is the word that tells them: I saw your kindness, and it made my day better. You have all four in you already — let us go use them."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four kind words — each one a thing you can DO."
  2. Walk the panels: the boy with folded hands is feeling kind, the girl hands a book to SHARE, the big kid HELPS the small one up, the girl says THANK YOU with clasped hands.
  3. Play kindness catch: toss a soft ball, and whoever catches it names one kind thing they saw today — any size counts.
  4. Assign one helper mission: "today your job is to help ONE person or toy." Report back at dinner.
  5. Close with the thank-you circle below and the takeaway: "kind hearts notice, kind hands do, kind mouths say thank you."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels show the words in action: Kind, a boy with both hands folded on his chest; Share, a girl handing a book to a friend; Help, a child steadying a smaller boy; and Thank You, a girl with hands clasped — each kindness shown by a child, not explained.

Ask your child

"What is the boy with folded hands feeling?" "What is the girl doing with the book?" "Who is helping whom?" "When did YOU say thank you last?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Sharing is letting my friend use it!" "I helped the baby!" or the observation: "The small boy fell and the big one helped him up."

Out in the real world

Kindness opportunities stack up all day: crackers to split, a sibling’s dropped cup, the neighbour’s bins, the librarian’s returned book. Narrate the ones you catch — "that was KIND" — and the words attach themselves to real moments.

Try it together

The Kindness Museum: at dinner, everyone places an invisible exhibit — "this is the time I shared my crayons" — and the family claps. exhibits can be from ANYONE’S day, including sightings of other people’s kindness. The museum never closes; it reopens every dinner.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which word means lending a hand? Which word do we say when someone gives? Is kind a heart-word or a hand-word?" Help, thank you, both — three answers and the kind words are theirs.

Parent tips

Never force the sharing of a truly precious thing — children learn generosity from what they CHOOSE, and guarding one special toy is allowed even in kind families. And catch yourself being kind out loud: "I am going to help Dad carry these" is a lesson in a sentence.

This lesson pairs with the Kind, Share, Help & Thank You flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Excited, Worried, Surprised & Proud — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson grows the vocabulary past the first four: feelings with bigger bodies and longer names, met in a book, a birthday and a wobbly first day.

What is this?

Excited, worried, surprised and proud are four bigger feelings: excited is joy with the volume up, worried is a what-if that will not hush, surprised is the feeling of OH, and proud is the tall feeling of a thing done well.

What does it mean?

Bigger feelings bring bigger bodies — wiggles, tight tummies, jumped chins, straightened backs. Children who can read those body signals early learn to know what they feel BEFORE it becomes behaviour.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: feelings show up in the BODY before the MOUTH (wiggles mean excited, tight means worried); surprised is the shortest feeling and proud is the longest; and worried is normal — everyone’s tummy talks sometimes.

Why this matters

These four bridge the everyday words and the tricky ones later in the class — worried especially, which is the feeling behind a thousand bedtime stalling tactics and one brave first day of school.

What it teaches

Interoception (sensing the body’s signals), emotion differentiation (telling feelings apart), self-awareness, and story comprehension — feelings words double as reading-comprehension tools the moment characters have problems.

Words to learn

excitedworriedsurprisedproudfeelingstummybrave

Say this to your child

“"Some feelings are big and some are sneaky. Excited is the wiggle one — your legs simply cannot keep still. Worried is the one that lives in the tummy and whispers what-if. Surprised is the fastest feeling in the world — it lasts one second and your mouth goes OH. And proud is the strongest one: it straightens your back when you have done something hard. Feel them all. Name them all. They are all yours."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four bigger feelings — feel them in your BODY."
  2. Act each panel: the huge grin (excited), the anxious eyebrows (worried), the round O mouth (surprised), the crossed arms and tall smile (proud).
  3. Play the body game: call a feeling, everyone shows it with their WHOLE body, not just the face.
  4. Tell one tiny story per feeling: the night before a birthday (excited), the first day of school (worried), a jack-in-the-box (surprised), a finished tower (proud).
  5. Close with the hunt below and the takeaway: "your body talks about feelings — now you can speak body."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels show the four faces: Excited, a boy with a huge open-mouthed grin; Worried, a girl with drawn-up eyebrows; Surprised, a boy with a round open mouth; and Proud, a girl with crossed arms and a tall smile — four feelings, four very different faces.

Ask your child

"Which feeling makes you wiggle?" "Where does worried live — the tummy or the toes?" "Which feeling says OH?" "What made you feel proud this week?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Excited is too much happy!" "My tummy does worried" or the story: "I was proud when I zipped my own coat."

Out in the real world

Feelings previews are everywhere: the wiggles before a party, the quiet before a haircut, the OH at a magic trick, the tall walk after a new skill. Name them in the moment — "those are excited wiggles!" — and the vocabulary sticks to real weather.

Try it together

Feelings Freeze: music plays, everyone dances; when it stops you call a feeling and everyone freezes AS that feeling — a proud freeze, a worried freeze, a surprised freeze. Last one standing is the Feelings Professor and calls the next round.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which feeling is the fast OH one? Which one lives in the tummy? Which one straightens your back?" Surprised, worried, proud — three answers and the bigger words are landing.

Parent tips

Worried deserves extra gentleness — never laugh a worry away; write it down, say it back, and answer one what-if with one real plan. And when your child acts proud, resist the urge to temper it: tall smiles at four are exactly the right size.

This lesson pairs with the Excited, Worried, Surprised & Proud flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Listen, Gentle, Take Turns & Kind Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is the manners course behind every good playdate: four habits that make a child the one others want to play with again tomorrow.

What is this?

Listen, gentle, take turns and kind words are the four daily habits of friendship: listening ears, gentle hands, turn-taking patience and words that leave people feeling bigger, not smaller.

What does it mean?

Play is a child’s first workplace, and these four habits are its professional skills — children who practise them get invited back, and every invitation is another chance to practise.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: listening means your MOUTH waits while your EARS work; gentle is a hands-and-words setting (soft with people, pets and small things); and turns always come back — waiting is just the queue, not the end.

Why this matters

These four are the most-used words in any preschool classroom — teachers say them fifty times a day because they are the actual mechanics of group play. Learning them at home means the classroom feels already-familiar.

What it teaches

Self-control (waiting), impulse management (gentle hands), turn-taking (the backbone of games and conversation), and prosocial language — the difference between "gimme" and "may I".

Words to learn

listengentletake turnskind wordswaitsoftmy turn

Say this to your child

“"Listen means your ears are the boss and your mouth is the helper — ears first, mouth second. Gentle means soft: soft hands on people, soft hands on pets, soft hands on the things people love. Take turns means the waiting is just part of the game — your turn always rolls back around, like the ball does. And kind words are the words that make people glow: well done, good try, want to play? Four habits. Practice them a minute a day and you will be the friend everyone asks for."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four habits that make you a great friend to play with."
  2. Read the panels: the boy with his hand cupped to his ear is LISTENING; the girl with wrapped arms is BE GENTLE; the raised finger and waiting hands are TAKE TURNS; the smiling girl is on KIND WORDS.
  3. Drill each one in a minute: one whole song of listening, one gentle stroke of a soft toy, three turns of a rolling ball, one kind word each at the table.
  4. Play the turn game below with the words spoken out loud — "my turn… your turn."
  5. Close with the takeaway: "gentle gets remembered; kind gets invited back."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels show the habits: Listen, a boy cupping a hand to his ear; Be Gentle, a girl wrapping her arms around herself; Take turns, a boy with a finger raised while a girl waits; and Use kind words, a girl speaking warmly — each habit shown at child size.

Ask your child

"What are the boy’s ears doing?" "How do gentle hands touch?" "What comes after MY turn?" "What kind word could you say right now?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Gentle is soft hands!" "Then it’s YOUR turn" or the generous one: "you can go first."

Out in the real world

The habits live in real minutes: listening to the whole instructions before building, patting the cat gently, waiting for the swing, saying "good job!" when a sibling finally manages the zip. Each one takes ten seconds and they stack into a reputation.

Try it together

Pass-the-Talk: a spoon gets passed around the table, and only the holder speaks — everyone else practises listening ears. The holder says one kind word about the person on their left, then passes. Two rounds and the kind words start generating themselves.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which habit is ears-first? What do gentle hands do? Does your turn come back?" Listening, soft, yes — three answers and the habits are in play.

Parent tips

Gentle hands work better as a reminder BEFORE the wobble than a correction after — whisper "gentle hands" as the pet approaches. And let your child catch YOU taking turns: "you waited for me — thank you!" reverses the teaching and doubles it.

This lesson pairs with the Listen, Gentle, Take Turns & Kind Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Breathe, Brave, Try Again & I Can Do It — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns courage from a personality into a ladder: four rungs any child can climb the next time something feels too big.

What is this?

Breathe, brave, try again and I can do it are the four rungs of the courage ladder: a breath to steady the body, a brave thought to steady the mind, one more try to steady the habit and the little sentence that holds it all up.

What does it mean?

Big feelings shrink when the body calms first — that is why breathe comes BEFORE brave. Children who learn the order stop waiting to feel brave and discover that brave is something you DO, one breath at a time.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: the breath comes FIRST (in like a flower, out like a candle); brave is a thought you THINK, not a feeling you wait for; and try again is the rung you may climb as many times as you like.

Why this matters

This ladder is the first calm-down tool of the class, and it is reused by every later card — the pause, the count to ten, the reset. Learning it early means the harder moments later have somewhere to stand.

What it teaches

Self-regulation (the breath), courage as process, growth mindset (try again is the plantable phrase), and self-talk — the sentence I can do it is the first one children learn to say to themselves.

Words to learn

breathebravetry againI can do itbrave breathsteadycourage

Say this to your child

“"When something feels too big, we do not have to be the bravest person in the world — we just have to climb the ladder. Step one: breathe. In like you are smelling a flower, out like you are blowing a candle — do it twice. Step two: think brave — what would the brave version try? Step three: try again — one more go, wobbles allowed. Step four, the best one: say it, small and strong — I can do it. Because you can. And if the first try wobbles? The ladder is still there. It never runs out."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the courage ladder — four steps up a wobbly moment."
  2. Climb it slowly: hands at the chest for BREATHE (in like a flower, out like a candle), fists up for BE BRAVE, forward lean for TRY AGAIN, fist up small and certain for I CAN DO IT.
  3. Pick one real wobbly thing — the big slide, a new food, the dark hallway — and climb the ladder out loud together.
  4. Tell the story of something YOU found scary and climbed: grown-up honesty is the best poster.
  5. Close with the game below and the takeaway: "brave is not a feeling you wait for — it is four steps you take."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels climb the ladder: Breathe, a boy with hands folded at his chest mid-breath; Be Brave, a girl in a little cape with her fist raised; Try Again, a determined boy with a raised fist; and I Can Do It, a confident girl with a small fist up — the four steps exactly as your child will climb them.

Ask your child

"What comes first — the breath or the brave?" "What does brave look like on this card?" "How many times may we try again?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Flower breath, candle breath!" "I can do it!" (the whole point) or the honest one: "I was scared and I did it anyway."

Out in the real world

Wobbly moments queue up daily: the tall slide, the swimming step, the new food touching the old food, the goodbye at preschool’s door. Climb the ladder at each one — quietly, quickly — and by the tenth climb your child starts it without you.

Try it together

Ladder Tag for Toys: line up three stuffed animals at the "too big slide" (a chair with a cushion). Each animal climbs the ladder out loud — breathe, brave, try again, I can do it — and takes the slide. Your child voices all three: shy voice, shaky voice, then the triumphant one. The third animal always makes it look easy.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is step one of the ladder? What do we say at the top? Does the ladder run out?" Breathe, I can do it, never — three answers and the ladder is theirs to climb.

Parent tips

Say the ladder with your child, never AT them — "let us climb it together" beats "just be brave" every single time. And celebrate the climb, not the landing: a child who breathed, thought brave and tried again SUCCEEDED, whatever the slide did.

This lesson pairs with the Breathe, Brave, Try Again & I Can Do It flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Smile, Care, Forgive & Friend — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson walks the friendship ladder in order — from the first smile that opens a door to the forgiving word that keeps a friendship mended and running.

What is this?

Smile, care, forgive and friend are the friendship words: a smile starts things, care keeps people warm, forgive mends the cracks after fights and friend is the name for everything the first three built.

What does it mean?

Fights are not friendship failures — they are friendship weather. The child who knows the mending word (forgive) learns that friendships survive storms, which makes them braver friends and calmer fighters.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: a smile is the friendliest thing you can CARRY; care means noticing when someone is sad or hurt; and forgive is the magic restart word — it turns a broken moment back into a game.

Why this matters

Every playground friendship runs this ladder weekly. Children who only know the top (friend) but not the mending rung lose friendships to ordinary weather — this lesson hands them the repair tool.

What it teaches

Relationship repair (the skill under every lasting friendship), empathy beginnings (care), conflict recovery, and the social courage of the first smile.

Words to learn

smilecareforgivefriendsorrymendstart again

Say this to your child

“"Here is the secret about friends: they still fight sometimes. That is normal — friends are just people who know how to find each other again afterwards. A smile starts it: hello, I am friendly. Care keeps it warm: I notice when you are sad, and I sit with you. Forgive mends it: after a fight, someone says sorry and someone says I forgive you — and the game begins again. That is the whole ladder. Smile, care, forgive — and the top rung, friend, takes care of itself."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is how friendships are built — and repaired."
  2. Climb the ladder: the beaming boy SMILES, the girl hugging a heart CARES, the peaceful boy FORGIVES with calm hands, and the waving girl is the FRIEND at the top.
  3. Tell a friendship weather story: two friends, one squabble, one sorry, one "I forgive you" — and the game continues.
  4. Play the mending game below with puppets so the repair script gets rehearsed before it is needed.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "every good friend has forgiven something — that is what the word really means."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels climb the ladder: Smile, a boy beaming; Care, a girl hugging a big pink heart; Forgive, a boy with peaceful closed eyes and clasped hands; and Friend, a girl waving hello — the four rungs drawn at child height.

Ask your child

"What does a smile say without words?" "What do we do when a friend is sad?" "What is the word that starts a game again after a fight?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Forgive means start again!" "I care about my teddy" or the mended one: "we fought but we are still friends."

Out in the real world

Friendship weather rolls in daily: the squabble over the yellow crayon, the friend who did not come to the party, the bumped tower. Say the ladder out loud in the small storms — "should we smile, care or forgive here?" — and the big storms come with the words already installed.

Try it together

Puppet Mend-It: two puppets want the same car. Fight! Then your child runs the repair: one puppet apologises, one says "I forgive you," and they invent a two-puppet game with the car. Swap roles and run it again — by round three the script is theirs and the fighting is just weather.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which rung mends a fight? Which rung starts a friendship? Can friends fight and stay friends?" Forgive, smile, yes — three answers and the ladder is standing.

Parent tips

Do not rush the forgive — it only works when the sorry is real. If your child is not ready, the pause is allowed: "we will find the forgiving word when we are ready." And model it yourself: children who hear grown-ups say "I am sorry I snapped — do you forgive me?" learn that mending runs uphill and downhill both.

This lesson pairs with the Smile, Care, Forgive & Friend flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Lonely, Loved, Frustrated & Relaxed — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson goes deeper than the first faces: four feelings every preschooler has carried without a name, and the relief of finally hanging words on them.

What is this?

Lonely is the ache of missing someone, loved is the warmth of being held, frustrated is the hot push when things will not cooperate and relaxed is the slow settle when everything finally fits.

What does it mean?

Lonely and frustrated are the two feelings that most often come out sideways — as clinginess, as explosions over small things. Naming them gives the feeling a door: it can walk out as words instead of breaking out as behaviour.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: lonely means I want someone who is not here (and it passes when they return); frustrated means my hands and the thing are arguing (not my fault, not permanent); and relaxed is a feeling you can BUILD with slow breath and soft shoulders.

Why this matters

This card is the class’s honesty moment: not every feeling is sunny, and the ones that are hardest to say are the ones most worth naming. Children who can say "I am frustrated" need far fewer storms to say the same thing.

What it teaches

Emotion differentiation at depth, interoception (noticing internal states), self-advocacy (lonely can ASK for company), and down-regulation — the relaxed word introduces the skill of deliberately calming.

Words to learn

lonelylovedfrustratedrelaxeddeep feelingssettlecalm body

Say this to your child

“"Some feelings sit deep. Lonely is the one that whispers when you want somebody and they are not there — at preschool pickup it always ends, because here I am. Loved is the opposite: the warm hug feeling that some children carry all day in their pocket. Frustrated is the hot one — when the block falls, the zip sticks, the lid will not turn, and your fists want to shout. And relaxed is the slow one: soft shoulders, slow breath, everything okay. Lonely, loved, frustrated, relaxed — four names. Now none of them has to shout."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four deep feelings — some warm, some wobbly, all allowed."
  2. Read the panels: the drooping boy is LONELY, the girl hugging a heart is LOVED, the clenched-fist boy is FRUSTRATED, the serene girl is RELAXED.
  3. Give each a body shape: lonely curls small, loved wraps arms around itself, frustrated squeezes fists, relaxed melts shoulders.
  4. Play the bedtime sort below — the day’s moments sorted into the four feelings, no fixing allowed.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "a feeling with a name is a feeling with a door."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the deep feelings: Lonely, a drooping sad boy; Loved, a girl hugging a pink heart to her chest; Frustrated, a boy with clenched fists; and Relaxed, a girl with closed eyes and a serene face — every one drawn gently, none of them scary.

Ask your child

"Which feeling is the warm one?" "What does frustrated do with its fists?" "When did you feel relaxed today?" "What helps lonely feel better?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Frustrated is when it will not WORK!" "I feel loved right now" or the deep one: "I was lonely at naptime."

Out in the real world

Deep feelings visit daily: the first minutes at drop-off (lonely), the bath before bed (relaxed), the shoe that will not go on (frustrated), the bedtime cuddle (loved). Name them where they live and the words become part of the day’s furniture.

Try it together

Bedtime Sort: four invisible boxes on the blanket — lonely, loved, frustrated, relaxed. Walk through the day out loud and drop each moment in its box: "the morning hug? LOVED box. The broken crayon? FRUSTRATED box." Then let your child sort YOUR day. No fixing, no lessons — the sorting is the whole game.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which feeling is the hot fists one? Which one melts the shoulders? What is the warm hug feeling?" Frustrated, relaxed, loved — three answers and the deep words are awake.

Parent tips

When the real frustrated arrives, lend the word, not the lecture: "this feels frustrating — the lid will not turn." The word in a warm voice works better mid-storm than any fix. And when your child says lonely, treat it as information, not criticism — company is the answer, right now, even just two minutes.

This lesson pairs with the Lonely, Loved, Frustrated & Relaxed flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Patient, Honest, Polite & Fair — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the four words grown-ups mean when they say good character — each one shrunk to something a four-year-old can practise before bedtime.

What is this?

Patient, honest, polite and fair are the character words: patient is the body that can wait, honest is the mouth that tells it true, polite is please-thank-you-excuse-me, and fair is the rule that everyone gets a turn — including the smallest.

What does it mean?

Character words are identity seeds: a child who hears "you WERE patient" starts collecting evidence of being a patient person. Four words on this card, four small identities under construction.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: patient is a BODY skill (hands quiet, feet still, breath slow) more than a feeling; honest might feel wobbly in the tummy but always lands softer than a lie; and fair does not always mean the same — sometimes fair means the little one goes first.

Why this matters

These four hold up every future classroom, team and friendship. Preschool teachers name them daily; this lesson makes sure your child arrives already speaking the language.

What it teaches

Delay of gratification (the famous waiting skill), moral development (honesty, fairness), courtesy as social lubricant, and rule-thinking — the first steps of understanding that rules protect everyone.

Words to learn

patienthonestpolitefairpleasethank youtruthturn

Say this to your child

“"There are four words that make you the kind of person people love to play with. Patient — your body can wait, even when your inside voice is yelling NOW. Honest — your mouth tells the truth, even about the broken cup, because people can trust your words. Polite — please, thank you, excuse me: small words that open big doors. And fair — everybody gets a turn, everybody gets a share, and the little ones sometimes get to go first. That is not rules. That is character — and it fits inside a four-year-old just fine."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four character words — each one a superpower you can practise."
  2. Meet the panels: the calm closed eyes are PATIENT, the hand-on-heart girl is HONEST, the folded-hands boy is POLITE, the chin-pondering girl is thinking about FAIR.
  3. Practise the waiting body: timer for one minute, everyone waits together — hands quiet, breath slow. That is patience, felt.
  4. Run one honest moment: ask a question with an honest answer built in ("was the broccoli nice?") and receive the true answer warmly — truth-telling must stay safe to practise.
  5. Close with the fair-shares game below and the takeaway: "character is just four words, practised."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the character words: Patient, a boy with closed eyes waiting calmly; Honest, a girl with a hand on her heart; Polite, a boy with hands folded; and Fair, a girl pondering with a finger to her chin — fairness shown as thinking, because fair takes thought.

Ask your child

"What is the patient body doing?" "Why is honest hard sometimes?" "What are the three polite words?" "What does fair mean for the little ones?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I waited the WHOLE minute!" "It was me who spilled it" (brave honesty) or the negotiator: "that is not fair — she had two!"

Out in the real world

Character moments arrive hourly: the biscuit tin on the counter (honest), the post-office queue (patient), the grandparent call (polite), the last two biscuits (fair). Quietly name them — "that was patient" — and the words collect real evidence.

Try it together

Fair Shares Café: one bowl of snacks, and your child is the server who must make it fair for everyone at the table — counting out equal shares, adjusting for the baby’s small plate ("fair does not always mean identical"). Pay the server in thank-yous — polite word practise built into the payout.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which word is the true mouth? What are the polite words? Does fair always mean identical?" Honest, please-thank-you-excuse-me, no — three answers and the character words are on duty.

Parent tips

Catch the truth gently: when your child confesses, thank the honesty FIRST, address the spill SECOND — children who are punished for confessing learn to hide, and the honest mouth closes. And let waiting practice be tiny and frequent: one minute a day beats one heroic hour at the supermarket.

This lesson pairs with the Patient, Honest, Polite & Fair flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Notice, Understand, Comfort & Encourage — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches empathy as a walkable path with four steps — because noticing someone’s feelings is a skill, and like every skill it can be practised by a four-year-old.

What is this?

Notice, understand, comfort and encourage are the four empathy steps: notice catches the feeling on someone’s face, understand works out why, comfort softens the hurt and encourage hands them courage for the next try.

What does it mean?

Empathy is usually described as a feeling, but for children it is a procedure — four small moves in order. Children who know the moves run them on friends, pets and parents, and the running changes them.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: feelings show on FACES and BODIES (the noticing); the best question is "are you… because…?" (the understanding); and comfort can be quiet — a sit-together is a full sentence.

Why this matters

This card is the class’s kindness engine: every later people-word — support, care, comfort, include — uses these four steps. Run them here on toys and teddies first, where mistakes are free.

What it teaches

Perspective-taking (the cognitive heart of empathy), emotion recognition in others, helping behaviour, and emotional first aid — the child-sized version of what nurses call a good bedside manner.

Words to learn

noticeunderstandcomfortencourageempathyfeelingshelp

Say this to your child

“"When someone is sad, our heart wants to help — but HOW? Four steps. First, notice: look at their face. Sad eyebrows? Dropped shoulders? Second, understand: ask gently — are you sad because…? Third, comfort: a hug, a hand, or just sitting close — comfort can be quiet. Fourth, encourage: when they are ready, the cheer — try again, I am right here. Eyes, question, hug, cheer. That is how you help a heart — and hearts remember everyone who helped."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four steps for helping a heart."
  2. Walk the panels: the hand-raised boy NOTICES, the chin-thinking girl UNDERSTANDS, the heart-hugging boy COMFORTS, the fist-up girl ENCOURAGES.
  3. Drill the sequence on a teddy with a problem (lost button, scary dream): your child runs all four steps out loud — "I notice you look sad… do you feel sad because the button is gone?… come here, I will sit with you… you can find it, I will help."
  4. Swap: the grown-up runs the steps for YOUR child’s small real wobble, naming each step as you take it.
  5. Close with the rescue game below and the takeaway: "first the eyes, then the question, then the hug, then the cheer."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels show the steps: Notice, an attentive boy with his hand raised; Understand, a girl nodding with a finger to her chin; Comfort, a boy hugging a pink heart; and Encourage, a girl cheering with a fist up — the helping sequence exactly as a child runs it.

Ask your child

"What is step one — eyes or hugs?" "What question helps us understand?" "Can comfort be quiet?" "What does encourage sound like?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I noticed my friend was sad!" "Are you sad because…?" (the full formula) or the tender one: "I sat with him until he felt better."

Out in the real world

Rescue missions appear all day: a sibling’s dropped ice cream, a friend’s skinned knee at the park, the dog hiding from the vacuum, a parent losing their keys. Run the four steps on small scale emergencies — the practice is the point, not the fix.

Try it together

Feelings Rescue Patrol: one stuffed animal per round "needs help" (a broken wheel, a lost spot, a scary noise). Your child is the rescue patrol and must run all four steps before the rescue is complete — the animal’s face must go from sad to cheered. Four rescues, four full sequences, one empathic pro.

Understanding check

Ask: "What comes after noticing? Can comfort be quiet? What does encourage do?" Understanding, yes, cheers — three answers and the empathy steps are in service.

Parent tips

Resist fixing fast — the understand step needs the question, not the solution, and children skip it because grown-ups model skipping it. Slow down deliberately: "I notice your face looks disappointed… was it because…?" And praise the noticing loudest of all: eyes that catch feelings are the rarest part.

This lesson pairs with the Notice, Understand, Comfort & Encourage flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Wait, Ask, Listen Carefully & Say Sorry — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is the playdate survival kit: the four words that keep toys shared, games fair and friendships intact when the wobbles come.

What is this?

Wait, ask, listen carefully and say sorry are the four smooth words: wait keeps hands still, ask turns grabbing into asking, listen carefully honours what people say and say sorry repairs the moments when hands moved too fast.

What does it mean?

Most toy conflicts are the same accident in different costumes — hands faster than words. These four words slow the hands down: the pause where a friendship can be asked for instead of grabbed.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: WAIT is the guard at the gate (hands still, one breath); ASK is the key ("may I have a turn?" works on almost every door); and SORRY is the repair kit — real, brief, and followed by changed hands.

Why this matters

Preschool is four words away from smooth: the children who can wait, ask, listen and repair are the ones teachers trust and children include. This lesson installs the whole kit at home, where the mistakes are cheap.

What it teaches

Impulse control (the wait), social negotiation (the ask), active listening, and accountability — the sorry that means something because it is modelled, never forced.

Words to learn

waitasklisten carefullysay sorrymay Iturnsgentle hands

Say this to your child

“"Here is how hands and words work together. Wait — when you want something someone has, your hands freeze and your one breath happens. Ask — then come the words: may I have a turn? It is amazing how often the answer is yes when the asking is nice. Listen carefully — when someone answers, or explains the rules, your ears take it all in before your mouth starts. And say sorry — when a hand moves faster than the words, sorry is the word that fixes it. Small word, big magic: sorry means I know I got it wrong, and I will do the asking next time."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four words that make playdates smooth."
  2. Read the panels: still hands WAIT, the raised hand ASKS, the ear-hand LISTENS CAREFULLY, the clasped-hands girl has a SORRY ready.
  3. Rehearse the ask with the toy game below — grabbing never wins in the rehearsal, asking always does.
  4. Run the listen test: give a two-step instruction ("get the ball, then the cup") and let careful listening earn the cheer.
  5. Close with the repair rehearsal and the takeaway: "wait, ask, listen — and when it goes wrong, the sorry is always ready."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the smooth words: Wait, a boy standing calmly with hands still; Ask, a girl raising her hand; Listen Carefully, a boy with a hand to his ear; and Say Sorry, a girl with clasped hands and a shy smile — each word shown at the moment it is needed.

Ask your child

"What do our hands do while we wait?" "What words do we use instead of grabbing?" "What do we do after sorry?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "May I have a turn — please?" (the jackpot) "I waited for the swing!" or the repaired one: "I said sorry and we played again."

Out in the real world

The asking life is everywhere: a sibling’s toy, the shared crayons, the question for the librarian, the turn on the digger at the sandpit. Each ask is a rep — and the grown-up who models "may I borrow you for a hug?" is teaching without teaching.

Try it together

Grabbing Never Wins: roll a ball back and forth with one rule — the roller must ASK before rolling ("may I roll it to you?") and the catcher must WAIT with still hands until the ask is finished. Every grab (yours too, playfully) restarts the round. The asking habit forms in about four rounds and generalises overnight.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do instead of grabbing? What do our ears do? What word repairs a mistake?" Ask, listen carefully, sorry — three answers and the playdates run smoother by the weekend.

Parent tips

The forced sorry teaches nothing but the flinch — instead, move close, speak low, and offer the words to borrow: "would you like to say sorry? here, I will help you start." And when YOUR hand grabs (the phone snatched from small hands, for instance), say the sorry yourself: the asymmetry is the lesson.

This lesson pairs with the Wait, Ask, Listen Carefully & Say Sorry flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Welcome, Include, Cooperate & Teamwork — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson takes kindness public: the four words that turn a group of children into a team, starting with the door (welcome) and ending with the cheer (teamwork).

What is this?

Welcome, include, cooperate and teamwork are the four group words: welcome greets the newcomer, include opens the circle wider, cooperate gives everyone a part and teamwork is the warm feeling when all the parts work.

What does it mean?

Classrooms and playgrounds run on these four words — the child who can welcome, include and cooperate becomes a social hub, and social hubs are looked up to, not left out.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: welcome is a HELLO plus a smile (it takes ten seconds); include means scanning for the one standing alone (the advanced move); and cooperate means everybody does a PART — nobody does everything.

Why this matters

This card turns all the private kindness of the earlier cards outward. Kindness to a friend is love; kindness to a stranger is leadership — and four-year-olds can lead.

What it teaches

Social inclusion behaviours, cooperative play (the developmental step beyond parallel play), task division, and group belonging — the feeling of being part of a we.

Words to learn

welcomeincludecooperateteamworktogetherpartgroup

Say this to your child

“"Groups are made of words. Welcome — hi, come in, we are glad you came. Include — you can play too; there is always room in a kind circle. Cooperate — we each take a part: you hold, I build, she finds the pieces. And teamwork — that is the feeling when it all works, the one that makes you shout WE DID IT with your whole body. Here is a secret: the strongest kids in any classroom are not the loudest — they are the ones who say you can play too."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four words that build a team."
  2. Read the panels: the waving boy WELCOMES, the open-armed girl INCLUDES, the ready boy is set to COOPERATE, and the two children arm in arm are TEAMWORK.
  3. Rehearse the hello: practise three welcomes — big wave, quiet smile, silly bow — all three count.
  4. Play the inclusion scan: "look around the playground in your mind — who is standing alone? What could we say?"
  5. Close with the fort mission below and the takeaway: "many hands, one team — and everybody does a part."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels build the team: Welcome, a waving boy; Include, a girl with her arms open wide; Cooperate, a smiling boy ready to pitch in; and Teamwork, two children with their arms around each other — the group words drawn at playground size.

Ask your child

"What does welcome sound like?" "What could we say to someone playing alone?" "What does cooperate mean — everyone does everything, or everyone does a part?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "You can play too!" "I will hold it, you build" or the proud one: "we did TEAMWORK!"

Out in the real world

Group moments fill the week: the new child at swimming lessons, the cousin visit, the puzzle that needs four hands, the cooking where one stirs and one pours. Name the roles out loud — "you welcome, I wash, she stirs — teamwork!" — and the words become reflexes.

Try it together

The Four-Hands Fort: a mission only possible as a team — a sofa-cushion fort that needs one holder, one builder, one fetcher and one inspector (rotate roles every five minutes). Halfway through, a stuffed animal arrives "new" and must be WELCOMED and INCLUDED with a job. Finish with the team cheer and the debrief: which word did the work?

Understanding check

Ask: "Which word opens the circle? Which word gives everyone a part? What do we shout when it works?" Include, cooperate, teamwork — three answers and the team words are live.

Parent tips

Assign inclusion as a job, not a virtue: "you are our Welcomer today — watch for anyone who needs a hello." Jobs feel doable where values feel vague. And when the squabbles come mid-build (they will), that is cooperate practice, not failure — teams negotiate.

This lesson pairs with the Welcome, Include, Cooperate & Teamwork flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Hopeful, Safe, Problem Solver & Kind Heart — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson installs the inner furniture: four words that describe what a strong day looks like on the inside, where nobody can see it but everybody feels it.

What is this?

Hopeful, safe, problem solver and kind heart are the inner-strength words: hopeful looks forward, safe settles down, problem solver looks for fixes and kind heart is the engine all three run on.

What does it mean?

Resilience is not toughness — it is the combination of hope (this will get better), safety (I am okay right now) and problem-solving (and here is what we try). Kindness is the fuel, because strong people who are also kind are the ones others lean on.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: hopeful is a feeling you can PRACTICE ("name one good thing coming"); safe is the feeling of NOW — nothing hurts this minute; and problem solver is a POSE and a question — hands on hips, what could we try?

Why this matters

This card is the deep pantry of the class: when the big feelings come — and they will — these four words are the shelf the calm-down skills sit on. Children who feel safe and hopeful try again; children who try again learn everything.

What it teaches

Optimism as a practicable habit, felt safety (the nervous system’s home base), flexible problem-solving (generating options, not just one), and character integration — strength and kindness running together.

Words to learn

hopefulsafeproblem solverkind heartstrongtryfix

Say this to your child

“"Inside every strong day are four words. Hopeful — I believe good things are coming, and I can name one: tomorrow we bake. Safe — right now, this minute, nothing here can hurt me; my body hears that and settles. Problem solver — when something goes wrong, I do not melt, I POSE (hands on hips!) and ask: what could we try? And kind heart — underneath all of it, the warm engine that does the fixing gently. Strong on the outside, kind on the inside — that is the whole secret, and it fits on one card."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four words for strong days."
  2. Read the panels: the cheering boy is HOPEFUL, the content girl is SAFE, the notebook boy is the PROBLEM SOLVER, the heart-hugging girl has the KIND HEART.
  3. Practice hope: "name one thing you are excited about tomorrow" — hope is a muscle and this is its lift.
  4. Strike the problem-solver pose together: hands on hips, chin up — then pose the problem and brainstorm two SILLY fixes and one real one (silly fixes are allowed because they make the thinking playful).
  5. Close with the takeaway: "strong and kind is the whole job — and you are already both."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the strength: Hopeful, a boy looking up with a bright cheer; Safe, a girl with closed eyes and a content smile; Problem Solver, a boy thinking over an open notebook with a pencil; and Kind Heart, a girl hugging a big pink heart — strength drawn soft, the way it feels from inside.

Ask your child

"What is one good thing coming tomorrow?" "How does safe feel in your body?" "What does the problem solver say when something breaks?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I feel safe with you." "What could we TRY?" (the pose, unprompted) or the hopeful one: "maybe the rain will stop by park time."

Out in the real world

Inner-strength moments hide in ordinary hours: the plant on the windowsill growing (hopeful), the quiet before sleep (safe), the ripped book page taped together (problem solver), the sibling comforted (kind heart). Point at the taped page: "that is what a problem solver did there."

Try it together

Silly Fixes First: pose a small real problem (the tower keeps falling, the cup is too full) and race to list fixes — but the first TWO must be ridiculous (bananas! a robot! a big pillow!). Silly opens the thinking door; the third fix is usually the real one, thought of by a child who is now laughing instead of stuck.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the problem solver ask? Which feeling means this minute is okay? What runs underneath it all?" What could we try, safe, kind heart — three answers and the inner furniture is in place.

Parent tips

Safety is built by predictability more than words — the same bedtime steps, the same goodbye ritual; the felt sense of safe comes from days that rhyme. And when the real fix fails, normalise it: "that fix did not work — good thinking though. What else could we try?" Problem solvers keep their tries.

This lesson pairs with the Hopeful, Safe, Problem Solver & Kind Heart flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Joyful, Tired, Confused & Curious — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson walks one whole day of feelings: the morning joy, the afternoon yawn, the homework shrug and the question that turns not-knowing into wanting-to-know.

What is this?

Joyful, tired, confused and curious are the four feelings of a full day: joyful is happiness with the whole body, tired is the yawn at the end of the tank, confused is not-getting-it-yet and curious is the lean-in that fixes confused.

What does it mean?

Confused and curious are the same face one second apart — teach them side by side and not-knowing stops being shameful. It becomes the front door of curiosity, which is the feeling all learning runs on.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: joyful is loud-body happy and it is ALLOWED; tired is not boring, it is information (the body asking for the bed); and confused is just curious that has not started yet — the shrug and the lean-in are neighbours.

Why this matters

These four cover the honest range of a real day — most feelings days are not one feeling but a parade of them. Naming the parade teaches the deepest lesson: feelings change, all day long, and that is normal.

What it teaches

Emotion granularity across a day, energy awareness (reading tiredness before meltdowns), learning attitudes (confused-to-curious reframe), and the meta-skill of noticing that feelings shift.

Words to learn

joyfultiredconfusedcuriousdaylearnquestion

Say this to your child

“"A whole day is a parade of feelings. Morning might bring joyful — the whole-body happy, arms up, maybe even a happy shout. By afternoon, tired yawns in — that is not naughty, that is your body asking for rest. New things bring confused — the shrug that says I do not get it YET. But look at confused’s neighbour: curious — the lean-in, the finger on the chin, the wanting to know. They are the same face one second apart! Confused becomes curious the moment you lean in. And curious is the feeling that learns everything."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "One whole day of feelings."
  2. Act the panels: arms-up laughing JOYFUL, the yawn with the floating Zz TIRED, the head-scratch CONFUSED, the finger-to-chin lean-in CURIOUS.
  3. Tell the day in four: the birthday morning (joyful), after the party (tired), the new puzzle (confused), then the leaning-in (curious) — and the puzzle gets finished.
  4. Play the day-in-four game below with YOUR real day — grown-ups act too, tired included.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "feelings change all day — and confused is just curious, warming up."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels walk the day: Joyful, a boy laughing with his arms thrown up; Tired, a yawning girl with a floating Zz; Confused, a boy scratching his head; and Curious, a girl with a finger to her chin — the parade drawn honestly, yawn and all.

Ask your child

"What does joyful do with its arms?" "Is tired naughty, or is it information?" "What is the difference between confused and curious?" "Which feeling did today start with?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Joyful is happy with jumping!" "I am tired-informationed" (close enough) or the reframe: "I am curious, not confused."

Out in the real world

The parade marches daily: the jump-into-your-arms morning (joyful), the 4pm slump (tired), the new rules of a new game (confused), the but-why streak (curious, gloriously). Name the weather as it changes — "oh, the tired just arrived" — and your child learns to read their own forecast.

Try it together

Day-in-Four Theatre: at dinner, everyone acts one moment of their day as one of the four feelings — no words allowed, faces and bodies only — and the rest of the family guesses. Grown-ups go first, honestly including a tired. Round two: which feeling do you want MORE of tomorrow, and how could we get it?

Understanding check

Ask: "Which feeling throws its arms up? What does confused become when you lean in? Is tired allowed?" Joyful, curious, yes — three answers and the day’s parade is named.

Parent tips

Honour the tired instead of fighting it — a child who can say "I am too tired to behave well" gets a cuddle; a child who melts gets a consequence, and both were the same feeling. And feed the curious deliberately: answer the but-why with "great question — how could we find out?" and confused never gets to feel like failure.

This lesson pairs with the Joyful, Tired, Confused & Curious flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Scared, Brave, Shy & Confident — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson takes the courage feelings out of the whisper-zone: scared and shy get names and respect, brave and confident get honest definitions — and the family maps where each one lives.

What is this?

Scared, brave, shy and confident are the courage feelings: scared wants to hide, brave goes ahead anyway, shy warms up slowly around new people and confident stands tall in its own skin.

What does it mean?

Brave is not the opposite of scared — it is scared that went anyway. And shy is not a flaw: it is a warming-up speed. Children who learn both facts stop apologising for who they are and start choosing who they are being.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: scared is a body alarm (fast heart, held breath) and alarms are information; brave is small and repeatable (one step, then another); and shy children are not broken — many scientists and writers describe themselves as shy.

Why this matters

The courage feelings are the ones children hide — which makes them the ones most worth naming together. This lesson gives permission for all four, and the permission is what builds the confidence.

What it teaches

Fear literacy (naming instead of hiding), courage as behaviour, temperament respect (shy is a speed, not a defect), and self-confidence built on honest self-knowledge rather than empty praise.

Words to learn

scaredbraveshyconfidentcouragealarmwarm up

Say this to your child

“"Everyone — every person, every grown-up — feels scared sometimes. Scared is your body’s alarm doing its job: heart fast, breath held, feet saying hide. Brave is not the opposite of scared. Brave is scared that decided to go one step anyway — and then another. Shy is the feeling around new people: quiet first, warm later — that is a speed, not a problem; some of the world’s best listeners are shy. And confident is the tall feeling when your own skin fits: arms crossed, smile up. All four feelings live in everyone. Even me. Especially me."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The four courage feelings — all of them allowed."
  2. Read the panels: the held-breath boy is SCARED, the fists-ready boy is BRAVE, the girl peeking from her hair is SHY, the crossed-arms girl is CONFIDENT.
  3. Draw the feeling map below: which things are scary-things, which are shy-things, which feel confident? The grown-up fills one in too.
  4. Tell one brave-but-small story: the first swim lesson, the lost-then-found moment — brave at four is small and that is correct.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "brave is scared that went ahead anyway — and shy is just a warming-up speed."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the courage feelings: Scared, a boy with worried hands near his face; Brave, a boy standing tall with fists ready; Shy, a girl peeking out from behind her hair; and Confident, a girl with crossed arms and a proud smile — none of them mocked, all of them drawn kindly.

Ask your child

"What does scared do to the body?" "What is brave — never scared, or scared and going anyway?" "Is shy a problem or a speed?" "Where do you feel confident?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Brave means do it anyway!" "I am shy at first" (the honest self-knowledge) or the question: "were YOU ever scared?"

Out in the real world

Courage weather arrives daily: the big dog behind the fence, the new Sunday class, the haircut, the dark corridor to the bathroom. Map them lightly in passing — "new places make you shy first, then confident, remember?" — and the map becomes a compass.

Try it together

The Feeling Map: a big sheet of paper, four zones drawn — scared-things, brave-things, shy-things, confident-things. The family fills it with real items: thunder (scared), the tall slide (brave), parties at first (shy), dancing in the kitchen (confident). The grown-up’s honest entries — "the phone makes me shy!" — are the most valuable ones on the page. Hang it; add to it; watch zones move over the year.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is brave really? Is shy a problem or a speed? Name one brave thing from this week." Scared-and-going-anyway, a speed, (their story) — three answers and the courage feelings are out of the whisper-zone.

Parent tips

Never call a shy child shy in front of them as an apology — "she is shy" becomes a costume they wear for you. Instead narrate the speed: "she warms up first, then the fun starts." And when scared arrives, do not argue the fear away — get curious about it: "what is the alarm saying? Is it a tiger-sized problem or a mouse-sized one?"

This lesson pairs with the Scared, Brave, Shy & Confident flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Share, Give, Care & Thank — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson maps the four shapes of generosity — because giving is bigger than sharing, and every child is generous in at least one shape already.

What is this?

Share splits something so two can use it, give hands it over for keeps, care holds someone close and keeps them warm, and thank closes the circle by naming what was received.

What does it mean?

Children who hate sharing a treasured toy often give drawings joyfully or care for babies fiercely — generosity is a shape-shifter. Four shapes on one card means every child finds theirs and gets named for it.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: share means BOTH keep using it (the toy comes back); give means it changes owners (and that is a big, brave kind of giving); and care is giving with your whole body — hugs, blankets, band-aids, patience.

Why this matters

This card deepens the early kindness words into a full giving vocabulary — the same words families, classrooms and eventually workplaces run on, practised here at snack time and teddy-bear scale.

What it teaches

Generosity in multiple forms (splitting, transferring, nurturing), gratitude expression, nurturing behaviour (care is the prototype of parenting), and the social warmth of a well-closed circle.

Words to learn

sharegivecarethankgenerouskindnesscircle

Say this to your child

“"Giving is bigger than one word — it has four shapes. Share: we both use it, and it comes back — the ultimate two-players game. Give: here, it is yours now, for keeps — the biggest kind of giving, and it feels strangely wonderful. Care: giving with your whole body — the blanket for the shivering teddy, the band-aid for the knee, the hug that fixes more than it should. And thank: the word that closes every circle — I received your kindness and I noticed. Four shapes, one heart. Which shape are you best at?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four shapes of giving."
  2. Read the panels: the two children SHARE one teddy, the boy GIVES a wrapped gift, the grown-up CARES for a small child, the boy THANKS with hands on his heart.
  3. Sort giving: hold up scenarios — "two kids, one truck: share or give?" "a friend is cold: which word?" "a birthday present: which word?"
  4. Run the giving circle below — one tiny act of each shape, in one sitting.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "giving has four shapes, and you are already good at at least one."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels show giving’s shapes: Share, a boy and a girl sharing a teddy bear; Give, a boy handing a wrapped gift to a friend; Care, a grown-up hugging a small child close; and Thank, a boy with both hands on his heart — the whole circle of generosity at child scale.

Ask your child

"What is the difference between share and give?" "What does care look like with a teddy?" "What does thank do to the circle?" "Which giving shape do you love most?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Sharing means it comes back!" "Here, it is yours" (a real give) or the nurturer: "my teddy needed care."

Out in the real world

Giving shapes stack through the week: the snack split between siblings (share), the flowers picked for the neighbour (give), the sick-day blanket runs (care), the thank-you for the library story (thank). Name the shape each time — "that was a real give!" — and the vocabulary multiplies the generosity.

Try it together

The Giving Circle: five minutes, four shapes. Share one snack between plates. Give one thing to the donation bag (chosen by the child — the choosing is the lesson). Care for one patient: teddy gets the blanket and the check-up. Thank one person out loud, specifically — "thank you for drawing with me." Ring an imaginary bell between shapes; the ceremony is what makes it stick.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which giving word means it comes back? Which one means for keeps? Which one uses hugs and blankets?" Share, give, care — three answers and every shape of their generosity has a name.

Parent tips

Never steal a give — when your child hands over their biscuit, accept it with the full ceremony or they learn giving lands flat. And protect the treasured-thing rule: sharing is practised on the ordinary toys; the one beloved bear is allowed to stay off-rotation while generosity grows on everything else.

This lesson pairs with the Share, Give, Care & Thank flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Be Kind, Helpful, Patient & Honest — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns four big values into four small jobs — because at four, character is not discussed, it is DISPATCHED: one kindness mission, one helper job, one waiting moment, one honest report.

What is this?

Be kind, be helpful, be patient and be honest are the be-words: kindness done on purpose, help spotted and given, patience practised in real queues, honesty told in real wobbly moments.

What does it mean?

"Be" words work differently from other words — they name the child, not just the act. A child who hears "you were patient today" starts collecting evidence of being a patient person, and identity drives behaviour far more than rules do.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: be-words are JOBS, not grades (small, today-sized, doable); helpful means SEEING the job (eyes first, hands second); and honest earns more than it costs — the true answer is always received warmly in this house.

Why this matters

This card sits after the feelings vocabulary because character needs a base: children who can name feelings find it far easier to be kind, patient and honest — the be-words are where the vocabulary becomes visible.

What it teaches

Prosocial identity formation, helping behaviour (initiated, not assigned), delay of gratification in natural settings, and moral courage — the honest report is a four-year-old’s first ethics exam.

Words to learn

be kindhelpfulpatienthonestmissionjobtrue

Say this to your child

“"Here are the four be-words, and each one is a job for today. Be kind — one kindness mission, your choice: a drawing delivered, a sibling helped, a flower found. Be helpful — eyes open for a job nobody asked you to do; helping first is the whole trick. Be patient — one waiting moment, felt on purpose: hands quiet, breath slow, timer ticking. Be honest — when the question comes, tell it true, even the wobbly parts; in this family, true answers are always safe. Do the four jobs and something funny happens: they stop being jobs. They start being you."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four be-words — each one a job you can do today."
  2. Read the panels: heart-shaped hands BE KIND, the teddy packed into a box BE HELPFUL, folded hands BE PATIENT, the hand-on-chest girl BE HONEST.
  3. Dispatch the missions: one kindness mission (child’s choice), one helper job (socks match, cushions returned), one waiting moment (the oven timer), one honest moment (a question answered true).
  4. Debrief each with the word, not the lecture: "you WERE patient. You WERE honest."
  5. Close with the takeaway: "be-words are not rules — they are costumes you can try on, and they start to fit."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels give the be-words bodies: Be Kind, a boy shaping a heart with his hands; Be Helpful, a girl tucking a teddy bear into a box; Be Patient, a boy with folded hands and closed eyes; and Be Honest, a girl with a hand on her chest — values drawn as actions, not posters.

Ask your child

"What is your kindness mission today?" "How do we spot a job nobody asked for?" "What does the patient body do?" "Is the true answer always safe here?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I WAS patient!" "I helped without being asked" or the brave one: "it was me who knocked it over."

Out in the real world

The be-words have job sites everywhere: the neighbours’ bins (helpful), the waiting room (patient), the who-drew-on-the-wall tribunal (honest), the sibling’s fallen tower (kind). Dispatch small and often — four tiny jobs a day build more character than any poster on the wall.

Try it together

Mission Control: each morning, pick ONE be-word as the day’s secret mission and write it where the child can see. At dinner, the family reports mission evidence — and everyone hunts for the mission in EACH OTHER. A week later, the child picks the missions for the grown-ups. Watching a four-year-old assign "be patient" to a parent is character education at its finest.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which be-word spots jobs nobody asked for? Which one tells it true? What do be-words become after enough practice?" Helpful, honest, you — three answers and the be-words are on the job.

Parent tips

Praise in the past tense of identity — "you were so patient waiting for the glue" — not "good boy": the first builds a self-image, the second builds a compliance habit. And when the honest report is hard to hear, thank the honesty before addressing the mess; the order of those two sentences decides whether honesty survives to age five.

This lesson pairs with the Be Kind, Helpful, Patient & Honest flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Forgive, Accept, Respect & Include — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is the deeper course of friendship: four words for the wobbles and the differences that every real group of children eventually meets.

What is this?

Forgive starts the game again after a fight, accept lets people be different without losing friendship, respect treats every person as valuable, and include opens the circle so nobody stands outside it.

What does it mean?

These four words make groups kind — a playdate of two only needs sorry and share, but a classroom of twenty runs on forgive, accept, respect and include. They are the civilisation words of childhood.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: forgive means the fight does not follow you into the next game; accept means different is allowed (different foods, different families, different speeds); and respect is NOT hitting, NOT mocking, and DO listening — even when you disagree.

Why this matters

The earlier friendship card taught the ladder (smile, care, forgive, friend); this one deepens it for real groups — the messy, wonderful, many-person world of preschool, where differences and conflicts arrive together.

What it teaches

Conflict recovery at group scale, acceptance of difference (the root of inclusion later), respect as behaviour (not feeling), and circle-keeping — the social architecture of making room.

Words to learn

forgiveacceptrespectincludedifferentcirclefresh start

Say this to your child

“"Friendship in a big group needs four strong words. Forgive — when someone messes up, we start fresh; the fight does not follow us to the next game. Accept — people are different, and different is allowed: different snacks, different homes, different speeds. Respect — I treat you like you matter: I do not hit, I do not mock, I DO listen. And include — the circle opens; there is always room for one more. Those are the words that make a group kind. Any group. Even this family."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four deeper friendship words."
  2. Read the panels: clasped hands FORGIVE, the open-armed girl ACCEPTS, the thoughtful boy RESPECTS, the welcoming girl INCLUDES.
  3. Play the open-circle game below — the circle literally opens wider every time someone is let in.
  4. Sort the differences: "some friends eat different food, some families have one parent, some kids talk later — is different okay?" (Always yes; different is the point.)
  5. Close with the takeaway: "forgive the past, accept the difference, respect the person, include the everyone."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the deep friendship words: Forgive, a boy with clasped hands and calm eyes; Accept, a girl with her arms open wide; Respect, a thoughtful boy with a hand to his chin; and Include, a girl welcoming with open arms — the group values drawn at child scale.

Ask your child

"What does forgive do with yesterday’s fight?" "Is different okay?" "What does respect NOT do?" "What does include do with the circle?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Forgive means fresh start!" "Different is okay" or the observer: "we let him play even though he is little."

Out in the real world

Deep friendship moments recur all week: the sibling truce after the storm (forgive), the friend who eats different food (accept), the quiet kid who hates being teased (respect), the newcomer at music class (include). Each one is a rep — name the word where the moment lives.

Try it together

The Open-Circle Game: four or more toys (or people) form a tight circle playing a simple ball-pass. A fifth toy approaches — shy, outside. The circle’s job: make the circle BIGGER, not tighter — include the newcomer, teach the game, pass to them second. Play three rounds; by the last one, your child is running the welcoming without a script.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which word starts things fresh? Which word makes room for different? Which one opens the circle?" Forgive, accept, include — three answers and the deeper friendship words are at work.

Parent tips

Respect is best taught by what it refuses to do — "in this family we do not mock, even when it is funny" — and what it always does: listen to the other side first. And separate forgive from consequences: "I forgive you, AND the rule still stands" is a sentence children need to hear; forgiveness is not amnesia.
