This lesson pairs with the Forgive, Accept, Respect & Include flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Pause, Breathe Deeply, Think & Choose Kindness — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the single most valuable move in the whole class: the pause that fits between a feeling and a reaction, in four steps a four-year-old can run.

What is this?

Pause, breathe deeply, think and choose kindness are the four steps of the pause: freeze the moment, slow the body, see what is happening and then — the best part — choose what happens next.

What does it mean?

Between the spark and the flame there is a gap. Self-regulation is nothing more mysterious than a gap wide enough to choose in — and this card widens it with two words (pause, breathe) and two moves (think, choose).

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: the pause is a FREEZE (everything stops, including words); the breath is the remote control (slow breath, slow body); and the last step is a real CHOICE — nobody makes you kind; you get to pick it.

Why this matters

Every calm-down tool in the class — the courage ladder, the count to ten, the reset — is a variation of this pause. Learn it here, at calm-home scale, and it will be there in the storm.

What it teaches

Self-regulation (the executive-function showpiece), impulse control, metacognition (thinking about what is happening), and moral agency — the child as the chooser of their own next move.

Words to learn

pausebreathe deeplythinkchoosekindnessfreezegap

Say this to your child

“"Here is the strongest four-step move I know. One: PAUSE — everything stops, like a statue, even the angry words. Two: breathe deeply — in through the nose, out slow, and your body hears it and starts to settle. Three: think — what is actually happening? (He did not mean it. The game broke. I am tired.) Four — and this is the magic: CHOOSE. Nobody makes you yell and nobody makes you kind. You choose. And when you choose kindness, you are the strongest person in the room. The pause is where the power lives."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the pause — the space where YOU choose."
  2. Run it small: someone says PAUSE — everyone freezes mid-motion (freeze dance style). Hold three seconds. Then one deep breath together: in through the nose, out slow.
  3. Add the think: "what is happening right now?" One sentence. Then the fourth step, spoken like a secret power: "and I choose kindness."
  4. Rehearse it on a pretend spark: "suppose your brother knocked your tower — PAUSE. Breathe. Think: he did not mean it. Choose: shall we build it again together?"
  5. Close with the freeze-dance game below and the takeaway: "the pause is yours; the choice is yours; the power is yours."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels run the sequence: Pause, a still boy with closed eyes; Breathe Deeply, a girl with a hand on her chest mid-breath; Think, a boy with a finger to his temple; and Choose Kindness, a girl hugging a pink heart — the whole gap between spark and choice, drawn in four frames.

Ask your child

"What is step one — freeze or fix?" "What does the deep breath do to the body?" "Who chooses the last step?" "What did YOU choose recently?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Pause means everything stops!" "I choose kindness" (wield it gently when they do) or the honest one: "I forgot to pause and then I remembered."

Out in the real world

Real sparks arrive hourly: the knocked tower, the taken crayon, the wrong cup, the end of screen time. Run the pause at each one — often silently, hand on chest as the signal — and the gap becomes a habit their body knows even when their feelings are loud.

Try it together

Freeze-Dance with a Choice: music dances, then stops — PAUSE! Everyone freezes; one deep breath together; the leader asks "how do we choose to play the next round?" and offers two kind options (gentle hands? new game? swap partners?). The children pick — the choosing is the lesson, dressed as a dance game. Rotate the leader every round.

Understanding check

Ask: "What stops first? What does the slow breath do? Who makes the last choice?" Pause, settles the body, me — three answers and the pause belongs to your child.

Parent tips

Practise the pause on calm days, never in the storm — the drill must live somewhere safe before it can work somewhere hard. And use the silent signal (hand on your own chest) instead of shouting PAUSE at a boiling child: the gesture says we do this together, which is the only version that teaches.

This lesson pairs with the Pause, Breathe Deeply, Think & Choose Kindness flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Proud, Disappointed, Grateful & Peaceful — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson covers the two feelings that follow every win (proud, grateful) and the two that follow every setback and bedtime (disappointed, peaceful) — the honest after-taste of a real day.

What is this?

Proud is the tall smile of a thing done, disappointed is the droop when the hoped-for thing does not happen, grateful is the warm thanks for what did, and peaceful is the quiet settle at the end of it all.

What does it mean?

Disappointed is the feeling nobody teaches and every child needs — small daily doses (the sold-out cookies) build the muscle for the big doses later. And grateful is its partner: the same day can hold both, and naming both is resilience.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: proud is celebrated out loud (tall back, told people); disappointed is allowed to be sad for a while — it shrinks when it is spoken; and peaceful is a feeling you can VISIT — the last minute before sleep is its front door.

Why this matters

This card balances the class: after the big feelings and the courage words, here is the honest ledger of winning and wanting — and the quiet that closes every day regardless of the score.

What it teaches

Achievement emotions (pride as motivation), disappointment tolerance (small-dose resilience practice), gratitude habit (the strongest single happiness habit in the research), and down-shift skills for the evening settle.

Words to learn

prouddisappointedgratefulpeacefulwinsetbacksettle

Say this to your child

“"Every day hands us four after-feelings. Proud — when you do something hard, your back straightens all by itself; say it out loud: I did it. Disappointed — when the thing you hoped for does not happen, the shoulders droop; that is allowed, and it gets smaller when you say it: I really wanted the park. Grateful — the warm feeling when something good arrives, expected or not; naming it doubles it. And peaceful — the quiet at the end, no wins needed, just breath and blanket. Proud, disappointed, grateful, peaceful: a whole honest day, four names."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The after-feelings — what follows the wins and the wobbles."
  2. Read the panels: crossed arms and a tall smile are PROUD, the drooped girl with a hand to her cheek is DISAPPOINTED, clasped hands are GRATEFUL, the softly smiling girl is PEACEFUL.
  3. Tell one story of each: the finished puzzle (proud), the rained-off park trip (disappointed), the unexpected biscuit (grateful), the last story before sleep (peaceful).
  4. Play the dinner ritual below — one proud, one disappointed, one grateful each, grown-ups first.
  5. Close with one peaceful minute and the takeaway: "same day, all four feelings — and that is a good day."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the after-feelings: Proud, a boy with crossed arms and a tall smile; Disappointed, a drooping girl with a hand to her cheek; Grateful, a boy with hands clasped at his chest; and Peaceful, a girl with arms open and a soft smile — the honest ledger of a day, drawn gently.

Ask your child

"What does proud do to your back?" "Is disappointed allowed?" "What does grateful do to a good thing?" "When does peaceful usually visit?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I am SO proud of my tower." "I am disappointed about the park" (the full word, working) or the nightly one: "I am grateful for… you."

Out in the real world

The after-feelings register daily: the mastered zip (proud), the closed playground (disappointed), the found parking spot (grateful), the lamp-off hush (peaceful). Grown-ups who say their own out loud — "honestly, I am disappointed the picnic got rained off; let us find one grateful thing anyway" — teach all four in one sentence.

Try it together

Proud-and-Grateful at Dinner: three questions, every night, everyone answers (grown-ups first, honestly): one proud thing, one disappointed thing, one grateful thing. Then thirty seconds of peaceful together — lights low, one slow breath. Two minutes total; the ritual does more for resilience and gratitude than any poster ever printed.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which feeling straightens the back? Which one is allowed to droop a while? What closes the day?" Proud, disappointed, peaceful — three answers and the after-feelings are on the table.

Parent tips

Do not fix the disappointed — rush in with a replacement treat and the feeling never gets its reps. Sit in it briefly, name it, trust it to shrink. And keep pride about the DOING ("you practised until it worked") rather than the being ("you are so clever") — process-pride survives setbacks, person-pride does not.

This lesson pairs with the Proud, Disappointed, Grateful & Peaceful flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Worried, Relieved, Jealous & Embarrassed — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson names the four feelings children hide: the worry that whispers, the relief that lands, the jealousy that burns and the embarrassment that blushes — all of them normal, all of them nameable.

What is this?

Worried is a what-if that will not stop, relieved is the phew when the worry ends, jealous is the hot wish for what someone else has, and embarrassed is the blush when everyone is looking.

What does it mean?

Jealous and embarrassed are the loneliest feelings of preschool — children carry them secretly, sure they are the only ones. The cure is not a lecture; it is a grown-up saying "I felt that too, last Tuesday."

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: worried is the brain trying to protect you (it just over-protects); jealous means you noticed something you want — and wants can be talked about; and embarrassed shrinks fastest when someone kind stays normal beside you.

Why this matters

This is the class’s bravest card: the feelings children least want to admit are the ones most worth naming together. A child who can say "I am jealous" at four is learning to bring shadows into the light — for life.

What it teaches

Worry literacy (naming the what-ifs), relief recognition (marking safety), envy vocabulary (jealousy as information about wants), and shame prevention — the early inoculation that embarrassment is universal and survivable.

Words to learn

worriedrelievedjealousembarrassedwhat iftricky feelingsnormal

Say this to your child

“"Some feelings play hide-and-seek. Worried is the what-if feeling: what if the dark, what if the first day, what if nobody plays with me — your brain is trying to protect you; it just shouts sometimes. Relieved is what lands after: phew — the worry was bigger than the thing. Jealous is the hot one: my friend has it and I want it TOO — that feeling is just information about a want, and wants can be said out loud. And embarrassed is the blush: everyone looking, wishing they would stop. Here is the secret about all four: every single person feels them — me, you, the neighbours, everyone. Named out loud, they get small. That is the whole trick."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The four tricky feelings — everyone has them."
  2. Read the panels: the finger-to-mouth boy is WORRIED, the eyes-closed relieved girl just felt the phew, the crossed-arms boy is JEALOUS, the blushing hunched girl is EMBARRASSED.
  3. Tell the grown-up stories below — one real, light story per feeling, told with a smile not a shadow.
  4. Practise the relief sound: "phew" — said out loud with wiped brows; relief deserves its own word.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "tricky feelings are not bad feelings — they are just shy. Named, they behave."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the tricky feelings: Worried, a boy with a finger to his mouth; Relieved, a girl with closed eyes and hands clasped in relief; Jealous, a sulking boy with crossed arms; and Embarrassed, a blushing girl hunched with clasped hands — every one drawn kindly, none of them caricatured.

Ask your child

"What does worried whisper?" "What sound does relieved make?" "What is jealous telling you?" "What helps embarrassed most?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Worried is a what-if!" "Phew!" (marking their own relief) or the confession: "I felt jealous when she had the bigger cake."

Out in the real world

Tricky feelings visit weekly: the stormy night (worried), the found toy (relieved), the sibling’s bigger slice (jealous), the potty accident at a friend’s house (embarrassed). Meet each one at its address — name it lightly, tell yours, move on. The lightness is the lesson.

Try it together

Grown-Up Story Swap: one feeling a night, four nights. The grown-up tells one true, small story — a worry that turned out fine, a jealous moment, an embarrassing tumble — told lightly, laughed WITH not at. Then the child may swap one of their own or just listen. No lessons attached; the stories do the teaching, and the safety does the rest.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which feeling says what-if? Which one says phew? Are the tricky feelings normal?" Worried, relieved, yes — three answers and the shyest feelings are out of hiding.

Parent tips

Never say "you have nothing to be embarrassed about" — to a blushing child that is one more person looking. Instead, stay normal: sit beside, carry on gently, let the moment pass in good company. And treat jealousy as a wants-report, not a character flaw: "you noticed you wanted that. Wants can be spoken. Want to tell me about it?"

This lesson pairs with the Worried, Relieved, Jealous & Embarrassed flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Notice, Name, Share Feelings & Ask for Help — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson condenses the whole class into one habit: the check-in — four steps that turn a storm inside into a sentence outside.

What is this?

Notice, name, share feelings and ask for help are the four steps of the check-in: notice what is happening inside, name the feeling, share it out loud and — when it is too big to carry alone — call for help.

What does it mean?

A feeling that gets noticed, named and shared almost never has to come out as a tantrum. The check-in is not one skill among many — it is the delivery system that carries every other word of this class to where it is needed.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: feelings announce themselves in the BODY first (chest, tummy, hot face) — the noticing is a body scan; the naming can start fuzzy ("something big") and sharpen later; and ask-for-help is not the last resort — it is step four of the design.

Why this matters

This is the engine card of the class: every feeling word learned so far rides on the check-in. Children who run these four steps daily need fewer meltdowns, recover faster and ask for help sooner — the trifecta.

What it teaches

Interoception (reading internal signals), emotion labelling under real conditions, self-disclosure (sharing is a social skill too), and help-seeking — the skill teachers and parents wish every child had installed.

Words to learn

noticenameshare feelingsask for helpcheck-inweather insidetoo big

Say this to your child

“"Here is the check-in — the strongest habit on the whole feelings path. Step one, NOTICE: put a hand on your chest and ask, what is happening inside? Something is always happening. Step two, NAME it: start fuzzy — something big — then try names until one fits: worried? frustrated? excited? Step three, SHARE it: say it out loud to someone safe — I feel worried. Step four, the safety net: if the feeling is too big to carry alone, ASK FOR HELP — can you help me? That is not giving up. That is exactly what step four is for. Four steps, two minutes, and the storm has somewhere to go."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The check-in — four steps from storm to sentence."
  2. Read the panels: the hand-raised boy NOTICES, the chin-finger girl NAMEs IT, the open-hand boy SHAREs FEELINGS, the clasped-hands girl is ready to ASK FOR HELP.
  3. Run the body scan: close eyes, one breath, "where do you feel something? Chest? Tummy? Face?" — noticing is scanning, not guessing.
  4. Practise the fuzzy-to-sharp move: "something big… is it angry? worried? excited? — let us try names until one fits."
  5. Close with the daily ritual below and the takeaway: "notice, name, share — and the fourth step is always there: ask for help."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels run the check-in: Notice Feelings, a boy with his hand raised mid-notice; Name It, a girl with a finger to her chin; Share Feelings, a boy telling with an open hand; and Ask for Help, a girl with hands clasped, ready to ask — the delivery system of the whole class, in four frames.

Ask your child

"Where do you feel feelings in your body?" "What if the name will not come — can we start fuzzy?" "What do we do when the feeling is too big?" "Who are your help-people?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "My tummy feels something big!" "I feel worried" (the whole system, working) or the request: "can you help me with my big feeling?"

Out in the real world

Check-in weather happens twice a day at minimum: breakfast ("what is the weather inside this morning?") and bedtime ("what was the biggest feeling today?"). Build the ritual at those two anchors and the steps carry themselves — storms get reported in sentences by the second week.

Try it together

The Feelings Weather Report: a pretend microphone, and everyone takes turns broadcasting their inside weather — "this morning in my chest: cloudy with a chance of grumpy, clearing after breakfast." Grown-ups go first with a real one. The child’s forecast may be silly; the noticing underneath it is not. Two minutes, twice a day, habit installed.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the check-in start — the body or the mouth? What if the name will not come? What is step four?" Body, start fuzzy, ask for help — three answers and the check-in is running.

Parent tips

Accept fuzzy names happily — "a big something" is a valid step two; precision arrives with practice. And make the help-people explicit: name three (and include one outside the house — a teacher, a grandparent), because a child who knows exactly WHO to ask asks sooner. Ask-for-help praised loudly is a meltdowns-later investment.

This lesson pairs with the Notice, Name, Share Feelings & Ask for Help flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Say Hello, Make Space, Be Curious & Ask Nicely — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is the joining-in kit: four words that open doors, save seats, start friendships and get things gently — rehearsed at home so the playground feels already played.

What is this?

Say hello opens the door, make space saves the seat, be curious asks about the other person, and ask nicely gets things without grabbing — the four smallest words with the biggest social mileage.

What does it mean?

Most friendships at four start with logistics, not chemistry: someone said hello, someone scooted over, someone asked a question. Children who own the logistics get more at-bats — and friendships are a numbers game at first.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: hello comes in all sizes (wave, smile, whisper — all count); making space is a BODY move (scoot, slide, make room) that says you belong here without a word; and be curious flips the spotlight — the fastest way to be interesting is to be interested.

Why this matters

This card turns the class’s inner words outward at playground scale: the feeling words become door-words. It sits right before the cooperation card because joining is step one; building together is step two.

What it teaches

Social initiation (the hello), spatial inclusion (making room), conversational curiosity (asking about others), and polite requesting — the may-I that replaces the grab everywhere it is installed.

Words to learn

say hellomake spacebe curiousask nicelyjoin inmay Iscoot

Say this to your child

“"Here is how you get into any game, anywhere. One: say hello — big wave, small smile, even a whisper; a hello is a hello, and it opens the door. Two: make space — scoot over, slide along, hold the blanket open; making room says you belong here louder than words. Three: be curious — ask the new friend something: what do you like? what can that truck do? Being interested in someone is the fastest way to become their friend. Four: ask nicely — may I have a turn, please? Works on toys, swings, crayons and almost every grown-up alive. Four small words. Whole friendships start with less."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four words that get you into the game."
  2. Read the panels: the waving boy SAYs HELLO, the hand-on-chest girl MAKEs SPACE, the wondering boy BEs CURIOUS, the folded-hands girl ASKs NICELY.
  3. Rehearse on toys (below) before people — two stuffed animals run the whole sequence: hello, scoot, "what do you like?", "may I borrow the crayon?"
  4. Practise three hellos in the mirror: big wave, quiet smile, silly eyebrow — all valid.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "the game does not start until someone says hello — be the someone."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the joining-in words: Say Hello, a waving boy; Make Space, a girl with a hand on her chest stepping aside; Be Curious, a boy wondering with a finger to his chin; and Ask Nicely, a girl asking with hands folded together — the kit drawn at playground-door size.

Ask your child

"What are the three sizes of hello?" "What does make space look like on a bench?" "What question could you ask a new friend?" "What works better than grabbing?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Hello — want to play?" (the whole door, three words) "here is space for you!" or the report: "I asked nicely and she said YES."

Out in the real world

Doors open all week: the new child at story time, the cousin arriving, the shared sandbox, the school open day. Run the kit in miniature on the way in — "shall we say hello first, or make space first?" — and let your child pick the door they open.

Try it together

The Toy Playdate: two stuffed animals meet at a tiny bench. Your child runs both roles (or you take one): hello (different voices are encouraged), make space on the bench, be curious — "what do YOU like?" — and ask nicely for the shared crayon. Swap roles, run it again, then retire the toys and deploy the same four moves at the real playground this week.

Understanding check

Ask: "What opens the door? What does make space say without words? What works better than grabbing?" Hello, you belong here, asking nicely — three answers and the joining-in kit is packed.

Parent tips

Resist scripting the friendship — hand over the four moves and let your child’s version be weird if it wants; a robot-dance hello that lands is worth more than a polished one that never leaves the house. And when the ask-nicely fails (it will sometimes), debrief the Ask, not the rejection: "good asking. Sometimes the answer is not yet — want to try again after her turn?"

This lesson pairs with the Say Hello, Make Space, Be Curious & Ask Nicely flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Share the Space, Work Together, Take Turns & Cheer Others — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson runs the full playdate: four words that handle the crowd — sharing the floor, building together, queuing for the good parts and cheering whoever wins the moment.

What is this?

Share the space, work together, take turns and cheer others are the four playdate words: room for two at the table, many hands on the build, my-go-your-go for the good parts and the cheer that points at someone else.

What does it mean?

Cheering others is the advanced course: a four-year-old who claps for a friend’s success has learned the opposite of jealousy — the feeling that quietly decides how good group life will be for everyone including the cheerer.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: sharing SPACE is easier and different from sharing things (room at the table, room in the game); taking turns means the wait has an END (my-go-your-go, then it rolls back); and cheering is a skill — specific beats generic ("you stacked the BIG one!" outcheers "yay").

Why this matters

This card is the group-practice run for everything the class has taught: feelings named, pause learned, kindness chosen — here it all meets other children, where the weather is real.

What it teaches

Cooperative and turn-based play, spatial generosity, waiting with an end in sight, and other-praising — the celebration of someone else’s success, which research keeps linking to lasting friendships.

Words to learn

share the spacework togethertake turnscheer othersmy goyour goyay

Say this to your child

“"Playdates run on four words. Share the space — the rug, the table, the game: there is room for both of us, scoot in. Work together — many hands build faster: you hold it, I stack it, we both cheer the tower. Take turns — the good parts are worth waiting for, and the wait has an end: my go, your go, my go again. And cheer others — when someone else does something great, YOUR thumbs go up: you stacked the BIG one! Here is the secret about cheering: it feels even better than being cheered. That is not a joke — try it and see."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four words that run a playdate."
  2. Read the panels: two children SHARE THE SPACE over one book, two more WORK TOGETHER with a high-five, the waiting boy TAKEs TURNS, the thumbs-up girl CHEERs OTHERS.
  3. Name the difference: sharing things (the truck) versus sharing SPACE (the rug, the table, the game) — space is easier to start with.
  4. Run the one-block-each build below — all four words in one game.
  5. Close with the cheer practice: everyone invents one specific cheer for someone else’s real success today, and delivers it.

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels run the playdate: Share the Space, a boy and a girl reading one book together; Work Together, two children high-fiving; Take Turns, a patient boy waiting with a hand on his cheek; and Cheer Others, a girl with both thumbs up — group life drawn at carpet-time scale.

Ask your child

"What is the difference between sharing a toy and sharing the space?" "Does the turn come back?" "What makes a cheer GREAT — yay, or you stacked the big one?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "There is room for both of us!" "My go — then your go!" or the advanced one: "GOOD STACKING, Mia!"

Out in the real world

Playdate mechanics repeat weekly: the crowded craft table (share the space), the bakery-shop game (work together), the single swing (take turns), the sibling’s first pedal strokes (cheer others). Each is a live rep — narrate the word as it happens and the mechanics become manners.

Try it together

One-Block-Each Tower: build a block tower where the ONLY rule is one block each, then pass — no exceptions, grown-ups included. Every placement earns a specific cheer from the previous builder ("tall one! perfect corner!"). The tower falls eventually (they always do) — rebuild rule stands, and so does the cheering. Five minutes, all four words, one laughing family.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we share besides toys? What do we say while waiting? Who is the cheer for?" The space, my-go-your-go, someone else — three answers and the playdate runs itself.

Parent tips

Cheering needs models more than instructions — a household that says "your brother zipped it himself — tell him what you noticed!" raises children who look for material to cheer. And keep turns SHORT at four: the wait is the exercise, so make the reps frequent and tiny; long turns teach only endurance.

This lesson pairs with the Share the Space, Work Together, Take Turns & Cheer Others flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Kind Choice, Good Friend, Try Your Best & Grow Together — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson hands your family growth language: four words that measure the day by growing, not by winning — and a bedtime rewind that collects the evidence.

What is this?

Kind choice, good friend, try your best and grow together are the growing words: the moment you picked kind over easy, the showing-up for someone, the honest effort (not the perfect result) and the getting-bigger that happens side by side.

What does it mean?

Growth language beats cleverness language in every study that compares them: children praised for trying choose harder puzzles; children praised for smart choose easier ones. This card installs the first vocabulary at family scale.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: kind choice means the pick was yours (nobody made you — that is what makes it strong); try your best is about the TRYING, and best changes day to day (tired-best counts); and grow together means the growing is a WE project — family, friends, everyone.

Why this matters

This card names the arc of the whole class: feelings learned, kindness chosen, and now — growing. It sits before the graduation cards because it gives the family the ruler to measure everything after.

What it teaches

Growth mindset language (process over person), prosocial choice-making (agency), effort attribution, and collective identity — the WE that grows, which is belonging’s twin.

Words to learn

kind choicegood friendtry your bestgrow togethereffortchoicegrowing

Say this to your child

“"In this family we have growing words. Kind choice — when you picked kind even though easy was right there: that was YOURS, you chose it. Good friend — when you showed up: sat with the sad one, waited for the slow one, shared the last one. Try your best — not perfect, just your all; and best is allowed to be tired on Tuesdays. Grow together — because nobody grows alone: we get bigger side by side, you and me and everyone in this house. Those are our words. Not how much, not how fast, not who won — did we grow? We did. Every day, a little."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The growing words — how we measure a day."
  2. Read the panels: the heart-hugging girl made a KIND CHOICE, the open-armed boy is a GOOD FRIEND, the fist-up boy TRYs HIS BEST, the sprout-cupping girl shows GROW TOGETHER — the only panel holding something alive and small.
  3. Ask the rewind questions (below) at bedtime — growth language installed in ninety seconds.
  4. Retire the word smart for a week: replace every "so clever" with "you worked until it worked" — feel the difference in the child’s posture.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "we do not measure days by winning — we measure them by growing."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the growing words: Kind Choice, a girl hugging a heart with closed eyes; Good Friend, a boy with his arms open wide; Try Your Best, a determined boy with a fist up; and Grow Together, a girl cupping a tiny green sprout in her hands — the only card in the class holding a living thing, because that is the point.

Ask your child

"What was today’s kind choice?" "Who did you show up for?" "What did you try your best at — even a tired best?" "What should WE grow tomorrow?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I made a kind choice!" "I showed up for Sam" or the planner: "tomorrow we grow a bigger tower."

Out in the real world

Growth evidence accumulates quietly: the stair climbed alone (try your best), the truce offered (kind choice), the friend waited for (good friend), the family plant watered (grow together). Name the evidence in passing — the child collects the identity; you just point.

Try it together

The Bedtime Rewind: three questions in the dark, every night: what was today’s kind choice? who was a good friend today (anyone, including you, including a story character)? what did you try your best at? Then one grow-together plan for tomorrow — one seed, chosen together. Ninety seconds, no stickers, no charts — the remembering IS the growing.

Understanding check

Ask: "What makes a kind choice strong? What is try-your-best about — the result or the trying? Who grows alone?" That it is chosen, the trying, nobody — three answers and the family has its ruler.

Parent tips

Guard the word best — best is not perfection, and a tired child’s best is still best; say so out loud or the word starts lying. And when the rewind finds nothing one night (some days are like that), the grown-up donates one: "I saw you pick up the baby’s cup — that was a kind choice." The ruler always finds something when someone else holds it kindly.

This lesson pairs with the Kind Choice, Good Friend, Try Your Best & Grow Together flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Calm Down, Count to Ten, Use Your Words & Take a Break — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is the emergency services: four moves for the stormy moments, drilled here on quiet days so they are there on loud ones.

What is this?

Calm down slows the body, count to ten gives the storm something to do, use your words sends the feeling out as a sentence and take a break is the honoured exit — step away, settle, come back when the storm is smaller.

What does it mean?

Calm-down skills are rehearsed, not wished for — that is why calm-down corners exist in every early-years classroom. A child who has PRACTISED the four moves on a happy Tuesday can find them on a furious Thursday.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: the body calms FIRST (soft shoulders, slow breath — words come after); counting is not magic, it is a JOB for the busy brain (ten fingers, ten breaths); and take a break is not a punishment — it is strategy, and coming back is part of the move.

Why this matters

Every class needs its fire drill. The feelings vocabulary, the pause, the courage ladder — all of it gets stress-tested here, and the four moves on this card are what remain standing in a real storm.

What it teaches

Down-regulation under arousal (the hardest self-regulation tier), sequencing (body before words), the counting strategy (attention redirection), and honouring limits — knowing when to step away is wisdom, not defeat.

Words to learn

calm downcount to tenuse your wordstake a breakstormsettlecome back

Say this to your child

“"Some moments bring a storm — and here are the four moves. Calm down: your body goes first — shoulders soft, feet still, one slow breath; the body is the rudder. Count to ten: one finger per breath, one… two… three… by seven the storm has usually lost interest. Use your words: now, with a calmer mouth — I am angry BECAUSE…; words let the feeling out the front door. And take a break: if the storm is still too big, you may ALWAYS step away — to the cushion, the corner, my lap — and come back when it is smaller. That is not quitting. That is strategy. Firefighters drill on quiet days too."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The four storm moves — for the days that go sideways."
  2. Read the panels: the folded-hands girl CALMs DOWN, the finger-counting boy COUNTS TO TEN, the open-hand boy USEs HIS WORDS, the beanbag child TAKEs A BREAK.
  3. Drill the body first: shake out the arms, then soft shoulders, slow breath — the body leads, the words follow.
  4. Count together: ten slow fingers, one number per breath — feel the speed drop around seven.
  5. Close with the calm-corner build below and the takeaway: "calm the body, busy the brain, say the words — and the break is always allowed."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the storm moves: Calm Down, a serene girl with folded hands and closed eyes; Count to Ten, a boy counting on a raised finger; Use Your Words, a boy speaking with an open hand; and Take a Break, a child resting curled on a beanbag — the emergency kit drawn comfortably, beanbag included.

Ask your child

"What calms first — the body or the mouth? What job does counting give the brain? Is take-a-break a punishment or a strategy?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Body first!" "One… two… three…" (mid-storm — the sound of it working) or the strategic one: "I need a break."

Out in the real world

Storms arrive on schedule: the tower collapse, the wrong-coloured cup, the leaving-the-park, the bedtime that came too soon. Walk the four moves through each real storm, slowly, beside your child — and on the quiet days, drill them with giggles so the moves feel like old friends, not strangers.

Try it together

Calm-Corner Dress Rehearsal: on a sunny afternoon, let your child choose the spot, name it (the Harbour? the Cozy Corner?) and stock the basket — one book, one bear. Then run the fire drill nobody needs: visit together for one slow breath while everything is completely fine, and leave while it is still nice. A corner rehearsed in sunshine works in rain; a corner met for the first time mid-storm just feels like timeout.

Understanding check

Ask: "What calms first? What is the counting FOR? Is take-a-break allowed?" The body, a job for the busy brain, always — three answers and the storm moves are drilled.

Parent tips

The grown-up’s calm is the curriculum: your slowed voice, lowered body and one audible breath of your own teach more than any script — co-regulation first, self-regulation later, that is the developmental order. And honour the break without ceremony: no sighing, no lesson on the way out; the break that works is the one that is just allowed.

This lesson pairs with the Calm Down, Count to Ten, Use Your Words & Take a Break flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

I Feel, I Need, I Want & I Choose — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson hands your child the four sentences that start with I — a voice that speaks feelings, needs, wishes and decisions without grabbing, hitting or whining.

What is this?

I feel names the weather inside, I need asks for what would help, I want speaks the honest wish and I choose owns the decision — four sentence-starters that carry a whole voice.

What does it mean?

I-statements are the peaceful alternative to grabbing, hitting and whining — the same message with the fighting stripped out. A child with I-words stops needing behaviour as a language.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: I FEEL is about inside weather (not "you made me" — just "I feel"); I NEED and I WANT are different (needs help, wants wishes — both allowed, said differently); and I CHOOSE is the proudest one — it means the decision is yours to own.

Why this matters

This card equips the check-in with sentence-starters: noticing and naming feelings (earlier cards) become SPEAKABLE sentences here. It is also the quiet alternative to every power struggle in the day.

What it teaches

Assertive communication (the healthy middle between passive and aggressive), needs-versus-wants differentiation, ownership language, and emotional expression in sentence form — the vocabulary of the whole class, armed with grammar.

Words to learn

I feelI needI wantI chooseI-statementmy voiceown it

Say this to your child

“"You have four magic sentence-starters, and every one begins with I. I feel — the inside weather: I feel sad, I feel excited, I feel that wobbly something. I need — what would help: I need a hug, I need help with the zip, I need you to listen. I want — the honest wish: I want the blue cup, I want a turn — wants are allowed; we just say them instead of grabbing them. And I choose — the proudest one: I choose this book, I choose to share. Four starters. When your words start with I, people lean in to listen — because you sound like someone who knows their own heart."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four sentences that start with I — your biggest voice."
  2. Read the panels: the chin-thinking girl says I FEEL, the open-armed boy says I NEED, the plain-spoken boy says I WANT, the confident girl says I CHOOSE.
  3. Model one of each, honestly: "I feel tired. I need five quiet minutes. I want tea. I choose the sofa."
  4. Play the I-statement dinner game below — one sentence per starter, everyone, grown-ups included.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "sentences that start with I are yours — nobody can interrupt your inside weather."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the I-statements: I Feel, a thoughtful girl with a hand to her chin; I Need, a boy explaining with open arms; I Want, a boy saying it plainly with crossed arms; and I Choose, a confident girl with a hand on her chest — a whole voice, drawn in four poses.

Ask your child

"Which starter talks about inside weather?" "What is the difference between a need and a want?" "Which starter owns the decision?" "What is YOUR I-feel right now?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I feel… jumpy!" "I need help, please" or the owned one: "I choose the green one."

Out in the real world

I-statement moments appear all day: the blocked view at the fence (I need to see too), the feared haircut (I feel scared), the shared crayon (I want a turn next), the outfit standoff (I choose the dinosaur shirt). Grown-ups who use them out loud — "I need ten quiet minutes, then I am all yours" — hand over the grammar for free.

Try it together

The I-Game at Dinner: four rounds, one per starter. Round one: everyone says an I-feel (real or silly). Round two: an I-need. Round three: an I-want — no judgement, wishes are wishes. Round four: an I-choose (about something small and real: tomorrow’s breakfast, the walk route). Grown-ups go first each round — especially with one real "I need five quiet minutes", which lands funnier than any lecture.

Understanding check

Ask: "What starts every sentence today? Which one is the proud owner one? Are wants allowed?" I, I choose, yes — three answers and the small person has a big voice.

Parent tips

Coach the difference without the lecture: needs and wants both get said, but needs get met faster — "you NEED a band-aid, you WANT more pudding; the band-aid is coming, the pudding is a maybe." And when the I-feel names YOU as the villain ("I feel angry AT YOU"), accept the feeling, reroute the sentence: "I hear angry. And I feel — what else? …worried? tired? Let us start there." The I stays; the blame goes.

This lesson pairs with the I Feel, I Need, I Want & I Choose flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Listen First, Think First, Speak Kindly & Solve Together — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the order that settles squabbles: not who is right, but what runs first — ears, then think, then kind words, then the together-fix.

What is this?

Listen first, think first, speak kindly and solve together are the four peace steps: full ears before any mouth, a thinking beat before speaking, kind words even in disagreement, and a fix both people can live with.

What does it mean?

Conflict is not the enemy of friendship — unhandled conflict is. Children who know the ORDER (ears, think, kind, together) turn squabbles into their first negotiations, and a four-year-old negotiator is a thing of beauty.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: listening goes FIRST because both sides need air (no interrupting — the hardest and highest skill); the think-beat is one breath between hearing and answering; and speaking kindly is not weak — it is how the strong actually win arguments.

Why this matters

This card is where the class meets real friction: two children, one toy, both certain. The feelings words set the table; this card serves the meal — the actual mechanics of two people finding the together-fix.

What it teaches

Conflict resolution sequencing, active listening under disagreement, prosocial assertion (kind AND firm), and joint problem-solving — the together-fix as the earliest form of compromise.

Words to learn

listen firstthink firstspeak kindlysolve togetherboth sidesfixfair

Say this to your child

“"Squabbles have an order, and here it is. Listen first — ALL the way to the end of what they are saying; ears open, mouth shut, even when you already know you are right (especially then). Think first — one breath between their words and yours: what did they actually mean? Speak kindly — you can be firm AND kind at the same time; roars make ears close, kind words keep them open. Solve together — not I-win, not you-win: the fix BOTH of us can live with. Two bears, one honey pot? Listen, think, speak kindly… and split it, or take turns, or find a bear who already ate. The order does the work."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The four steps that settle any squabble."
  2. Read the panels: the ear-hand girl LISTENs FIRST, the chin-thinking boy THINKs FIRST, the open-hand boy SPEAKs KINDLY, the two facing children SOLVE TOGETHER.
  3. Drill the order with a prop squabble: two bears, one honey pot. You narrate each step as the bears run it — ears (each bear says what it heard the other say), think (one breath), kind (no roars), together (both bears’ fix).
  4. Deploy it on the next real dispute as the narrator: you speak the step-names, the children do the steps.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "the fix is never me-win — it is us-fixed."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels run the peace process: Listen First, a girl listening with a hand to her ear; Think First, a boy pondering with a finger to his chin; Speak Kindly, a boy talking with an open friendly hand; and Solve Together, two children talking face to face — the order drawn exactly as it should be run.

Ask your child

"What comes before the mouth?" "How long is the think-first beat?" "Can you be firm and kind at the same time?" "Whose fix is it in the end?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Ears first!" "Let me think for a second" (the beat, arriving) or the negotiated one: "we could take turns AND share the top."

Out in the real world

Disputes queue up daily: the swing, the front seat, the last sticker, the loudest singer. Run the order as narrator on the small ones — naming each step as it happens — and by the umpteenth small one, the children run the steps without you. Then retire gracefully to the refreshments.

Try it together

The Bear Court: a squabble is brought before the family’s wisest bear (a teddy on a cushion). The bear (voiced by your child, ideally) enforces the order: each side speaks, the OTHER side must say back what it heard, one think-breath, kind words only, then the together-fix proposed by the cubs themselves. Bear adjourns with a gavel paw. Silly, sacred, and it teaches the sequence better than any diagram.

Understanding check

Ask: "What runs first? What sits between hearing and answering? Whose fix wins?" Ears, one breath, both of us — three answers and the peace process is in service.

Parent tips

Narrate the steps, not the verdict: "that was listen-first… now the think-breath…" — children doing the steps need the step-names, not a judge. And when the together-fix is lopsided (always give the little one the honey), let it stand: fairness calibrates over months of practice, and a fix both AGREED to is the lesson, whatever the honey math.

This lesson pairs with the Listen First, Think First, Speak Kindly & Solve Together flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Welcome All, Be Inclusive, Share Joy & Make a Friend — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is the open-door policy in child size: four words that make a child the one who greets, gathers, glows and — sometimes before dinner — makes a friend.

What is this?

Welcome all greets every comer, be inclusive scans for the one standing alone, share joy hands happiness over out loud, and make a friend is the day’s best possible achievement.

What does it mean?

Inclusion is kindness aimed at a group: the child who notices the left-out one and opens the circle is doing social leadership at four. The world runs on exactly this, and it starts here, at the sandbox.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: welcome ALL means no auditions (nobody has to be funny or fast to get a hello); be inclusive is a SCANNING skill — eyes up, notice who is alone; and joy is contagious on purpose — a shared "look at THIS!" doubles on the spot.

Why this matters

This card gathers the joining-in kit (say hello, make space) and the group words (include, cooperate) into one open-door habit — the final social skill before the belonging cards close the class.

What it teaches

Social leadership (initiating inclusion), empathy in action (noticing the outsider), joy expression (shared delight as social glue), and friendship formation skills — the actual mechanics of the first friend.

Words to learn

welcome allbe inclusiveshare joymake a friendhelloalonetogether

Say this to your child

“"Here is the open-door way to play. Welcome ALL — every single person gets a hello; no tryouts, no auditions: the fast one, the slow one, the new one, the loud one. Be inclusive — keep your eyes up: if someone is standing alone, you are the one who walks over — you can play too is the strongest sentence on any playground. Share joy — when something delights you, DELIVER it: look at this! Joy given away comes back doubled; that is its whole magic. And make a friend — today, this week, at your own speed. Someone opened a door for your first friend. Now you know how the door works."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The open-door words."
  2. Read the panels: the wide-armed girl WELCOMEs ALL, the heart-hugging boy BEs INCLUSIVE, the fist-up boy SHAREs JOY, the waving girl MAKEs A FRIEND.
  3. Rehearse the scan: "imagine the playground — who is standing alone? What are three things we could say or do?"
  4. Practise the joy-share: one child shows a treasure (a drawing, a shell), the family responds with real delight — joy grows when it lands.
  5. Close with the inclusion mission below and the takeaway: "the door does not open itself — someone opens it. Be the someone."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels open the door: Welcome All, a girl with her arms open wide; Be Inclusive, a boy hugging a pink heart; Share Joy, a boy cheering with a fist up; and Make a Friend, a girl waving hello — the open-door policy drawn at sandbox scale.

Ask your child

"Who gets a hello under welcome all?" "What do your eyes do when you are being inclusive?" "What happens to joy when you give it away?" "Who opened a door for you once?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Nobody plays alone!" "Look what I found — come SEE!" or the mission report: "I said hi to the new girl and she likes unicorns TOO."

Out in the real world

Open-door moments arrive weekly: the new starter at swimming, the birthday party where someone knows nobody, the park at busy hour, the family gathering with the shy cousin. Pre-brief lightly ("want a mission or just a hello today?") and debrief gently — the door-words need reps, not pressure.

Try it together

The Inclusion Mission: once a week, one official mission — at the park, the class, the gathering, be the one who says hello to someone new or brings the standing-alone child into the game. Choose the mission together, keep it small (one hello counts), and debrief at dinner: how did it feel to open the door? The answer — usually proud, sometimes shy — is the growth, spoken aloud.

Understanding check

Ask: "Does welcome all have tryouts? What are your eyes doing when they are being inclusive? What happens to shared joy?" No, scanning, it doubles — three answers and the door is theirs to open.

Parent tips

Let the mission be optional — inclusion chosen freely sticks; inclusion assigned sours. And when your child reports a failed hello (the other child walked off), treat it as weather, not verdict: "sometimes doors take three tries. The opening still counts." Door-openers need their courage protected more than their success rates.

This lesson pairs with the Welcome All, Be Inclusive, Share Joy & Make a Friend flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

You Matter, I Am Here, You Are Safe & We Care — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is the family’s anchor: four sentences said on the hard days until they become the voice your child carries inside their own head.

What is this?

You matter, I am here, you are safe and we care are the four reassurance sentences: worth declared, presence promised, safety named and belonging wrapped around all of it.

What does it mean?

Reassurance works by rhythm and repetition, not novelty — the SAME four sentences on every hard day become internalised. A child who has heard you-are-safe a thousand calm times can find it once in a storm.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: you matter is unconditional (not you matter WHEN you behave — just you matter); I am here is a promise about presence, not a promise about never leaving (I come back is the goodbye version); and these words are TRANSFERABLE — your child can offer them to a friend, a baby, a teddy, even you.

Why this matters

This card is the class’s heart: every feeling word, calm-down skill and kindness habit rests on the floor these four sentences build. It sits with the belonging cards because it IS belonging, spoken.

What it teaches

Secure attachment language, felt safety (the nervous system’s home), unconditional worth (worth separate from behaviour), and comforting Others — the child as giver of the same four sentences.

Words to learn

you matterI am hereyou are safewe carereassurancecome backbelong

Say this to your child

“"There are four sentences I will say to you on every hard day, and plenty of easy ones. You matter — exactly as you are, on your best day and your worst, no conditions attached. I am here — right beside you; and when I must go, the promise becomes I come back, and I always do. You are safe — this minute, this room, these arms: nothing here can hurt you. And we care — the whole family, a whole row of people, all facing your direction. Say them back to me when you learn them. Give them to your teddy. Give them to a friend who falls. These words are not just for receiving — they are for carrying."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The four sentences — for hard days and every day."
  2. Read the panels: the clasped-hands girl says YOU MATTER, the reaching boy says I AM HERE, the peaceful boy says YOU ARE SAFE, the heart-hands girl says WE CARE.
  3. Say all four to your child, slowly, on an ordinary day — reassurance must not live only in emergencies.
  4. Teach them as GIFTS: practise offering them to a teddy after a fall ("you matter, I am here, you are safe, we care") — children give comfort brilliantly when handed the words.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "these four sentences are yours to hear, and yours to give."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the sentences: You Matter, a girl with warm clasped hands; I Am Here, a boy reaching out a steadying arm; You Are Safe, a boy with closed eyes, calm; and We Care, a girl shaping a heart with her hands — the anchor drawn simply, the way the sentences are said.

Ask your child

"What are the four sentences?" "What does I-am-here become when I have to leave?" "Who else could we say them to?" "Do they still count on a grumpy day?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "You matter, teddy. I am here." (the whole gift, delivered) "you came back!" or the question: "say the safe one again."

Out in the real world

Anchor moments repeat: the nightmare at 3am (you are safe, I am here), the preschool goodbye (I come back — after lunch, I promise), the scraped knee (you matter, we care), the ordinary Tuesday for no reason at all (all four, just because). The ordinary-day repetitions are the ones that build the storm-time voice.

Try it together

Pass the Sentences: a soft ball passed around the circle (toys included) — the holder receives all four sentences from the group, then passes. Round two: the holder SAYS the four to the next holder. By round three, your child is comforting a stuffed rabbit with the full sequence, and the sentences are officially theirs — to hear, and to give.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the four sentences. What does the promise become when you leave? Who can give these words?" You-matter-I-am-here-you-are-safe-we-care, I come back, anyone — three answers and the anchor holds.

Parent tips

Keep the sentences UNCONDITIONAL — you matter after the tantrum counts double, because that is when a child most needs to know worth is not on trial. And when you must leave, never swap I am here for silence: the goodbye ritual (I come back, I always do, watch the clock with me) is the same anchor in its travel shape.

This lesson pairs with the You Matter, I Am Here, You Are Safe & We Care flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Keep Trying, Learn, Celebrate & Be Yourself — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson builds the confidence shelf: four words that carry a child through the wobbles of learning anything — and one family ritual that makes sure the wins get their moment.

What is this?

Keep trying walks through the wobble, learn harvests every attempt, celebrate marks the wins (small ones loudest) and be yourself is the standing rule underneath: there is only one you, and that is the good news.

What does it mean?

Celebrate is the most skipped word in child-rearing — progress that is never marked quietly stops. A family that cheers small wins out loud raises children who attempt big things, because the trying has learned it leads somewhere good.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: wobbles are PART of trying, not a verdict on you; every attempt teaches something (the learn is automatic once you look for it); and being yourself is not the last step — it is the ground all four words stand on.

Why this matters

This card is the stamina of the class: feelings named, kindness chosen, skills drilled — and here is the fuel that keeps a child going when the zip sticks on the fortieth attempt. It also pre-loads the graduation: be yourself is what the whole path was for.

What it teaches

Persistence (the continue-through-difficulty muscle), learning orientation (attempt as data), celebration habits (marked progress sustains motivation), and self-acceptance — identity as the base camp for all achievement.

Words to learn

keep tryinglearncelebratebe yourselfwobblewinonly one you

Say this to your child

“"Here are the four words that make hard things possible. Keep trying — the wobble is part of it; every climber slips, every drawer sticks, every zip fights back on the first try. Learn — every attempt teaches something, even the ones that flop; especially those. Celebrate — when something lands, MARK it: cheer, dance, tell Dad, tell the neighbour’s cat; small wins counted loudly are what keep the trying coming. And be yourself — underneath everything, the standing rule: there is only one you in the whole world, and your way of doing things is allowed to be yours. Wobble, learn, celebrate — and stay you. That is the whole confidence recipe."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The confidence words."
  2. Read the panels: the fist-up girl KEEPs TRYING, the question-mark boy LEARNs, the sparkling boy CELEBRATEs, the thumbs-up winking girl BEs HERSELF.
  3. Tell the wobble story: something you failed at first, tried again, and what the second attempt taught — grown-up wobbles are the best teaching material in the house.
  4. Hold the celebration below — one HARD thing, cheered properly, effort named as the hero.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "wobble, learn, celebrate, repeat — and stay you the whole time."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the confidence: Keep Trying, a girl with a determined fist up; Learn, a wondering boy with a question mark over his head; Celebrate, a boy cheering under little sparkles; and Be Yourself, a winking girl with her thumb up — effort drawn as the hero, sparkle and all.

Ask your child

"What is a wobble — a stop sign or part of trying?" "What does a flopped attempt teach?" "Which wins do we celebrate — only the big ones?" "What is something ONLY you do?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Wobbles are part of it!" "I learned the wet sponge slips" (harvested) or the self-knowledge: "I do my dancing silly and that is MY way."

Out in the real world

Confidence moments stack daily: the shoe attempt (forty tries), the tower collapse, the first pedal stroke, the wobbly note at singing time. Mark each with the right word — "you kept trying," "what did that teach us," "CELEBRATE!" — and the words become the child’s inner soundtrack by default.

Try it together

The Hard-Thing Celebration: once a week, the family celebrates one HARD thing — confetti optional, cheering mandatory. The rule: the thing must have involved wobbles. Each person tells theirs (grown-ups first: the jammed printer counts), the effort is named as the hero ("you tried four ways!"), and the celebration is real: a dance, a dessert, a lap of the table. Effort that gets celebrated comes back for more.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are wobbles — part of it or a stop sign? Which wins get celebrated? What is the rule underneath all four?" Part of it, all of them (small ones loudest), be yourself — three answers and the confidence shelf is loaded.

Parent tips

Celebrate the specific, not the superlative — "you tried the zipper upside down AND the right way" beats "amazing!" every time; specificity proves you actually watched. And guard be-yourself from becoming a costume: the winking, thumbs-up child on the card is not a requirement — your quiet child’s be-yourself might look like standing at the edge of the party, watching, until ready. That counts. That is the word working.

This lesson pairs with the Keep Trying, Learn, Celebrate & Be Yourself flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Welcome, Belong, Trust & Connect — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson begins the graduation: four words about WE — the open door, the fixed spot, the kept promise and the thread that runs underneath every one of them.

What is this?

Welcome opens the door, belong finds the seat that is yours, trust keeps the promises that hold, and connect is the checking-in thread that runs underneath all three.

What does it mean?

Belonging is not a mood that appears — it is built out of small fixed things: a coat hook with a name, a cup that is always theirs, a goodbye that always comes with a return. Children who can NAME their belonging carry it anywhere.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: welcome is a door you can HOLD for others now (you know how it feels to be welcomed — pass it on); belong is made of EVIDENCE (hooks, cups, seats, songs — pointable things); and trust is kept promises, small ones most of all.

Why this matters

The class closes its circle here: the feelings words named the inside, the kindness words aimed outward — and the belonging words name the WE that holds it all. Everything after this card is harvest.

What it teaches

Sense of belonging (the strongest single protective factor in child development research), trust-building through reliability, family identity (the we), and welcoming agency — the child as door-holder for others.

Words to learn

welcomebelongtrustconnectfamilypromisemy spot

Say this to your child

“"Four words hold our family up. Welcome — you are wanted here, always; the door is not locked to you, not ever. Belong — this is your hook, your cup, your seat, your bedtime song; you are not a guest here, you are a beam in the house. Trust — I keep my word to you, small word, small promises especially: the sticker saved, the park kept, the return on time. And connect — we check in, we laugh at the same silly thing, we are us. Four beams. And you — you get to hold the door for others now, because you know exactly how it feels from the inside."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The four WE words."
  2. Read the panels: the waving girl WELCOMEs, the content boy BELONGs, the hand-on-heart girl TRUSTs, the open-armed boy CONNECTs.
  3. Run the belonging hunt below — find the child’s name (literally or figuratively) all over the house.
  4. Make one small trust-promise today and keep it visibly: "I said I would save you the sticker — here it is." Trust is built at sticker scale.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "welcome, belong, trust, connect — four beams, one house, and you live in it."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the WE: Welcome, a waving girl; Belong, a content boy with hands clasped; Trust, a girl with a hand on her heart; and Connect, a boy reaching out with open arms — the family’s beams, drawn warmly.

Ask your child

"Where is your spot in this house?" "What is a promise kept this week?" "What does connect look like in our family?" "Who could WE welcome this week?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "That is MY hook!" "you kept your promise!" (trust, noticed) or the pass-it-on: "can my friend come in? I will hold the door."

Out in the real world

Belonging evidence fills the house: the toothbrush with the favourite colour, the drawing taped at child height, the same three books at bedtime, the seat that is always theirs in the car. Point at them occasionally — "yours, yours, yours" — and the abstract word becomes a house tour.

Try it together

The Belonging Hunt: walk the house with a detective’s eye and find ten pieces of belonging evidence — the hook, the cup, the shoe spot, the bedtime song, the drawing on the wall, the family photo, the garden patch, the car seat, the snack shelf, the always-yours chair. Photograph or draw the best ones into a little book titled WHERE I BELONG. Belonging, once you hunt it, turns out to have been everywhere.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which word means the seat is yours? What is trust made of? Who holds the door now?" Belong, kept promises, you do — three answers and the house stands.

Parent tips

Build trust at the smallest scale — children audit promises at four with forensic seriousness, so promise LESS and keep MORE; a kept sticker-promise outweighs a hundred lectures on reliability. And when the family welcomes a guest, hand your child the door: the welcomed child who becomes the welcomer has completed the entire lesson without noticing it was a lesson.

This lesson pairs with the Welcome, Belong, Trust & Connect flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Notice, Pause, Breathe & Reset — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson gives your family a single, blame-free power move: the RESET — four steps that stop a going-sideways moment and start it again, fresh, no guilt attached.

What is this?

Notice spots the moment tipping, pause stops everything mid-motion, breathe runs one slow breath through the group, and reset starts the bit again from the top — same game, fresh start, nobody in trouble.

What does it mean?

Most meltdowns spiral because nobody has a word that stops them without blame. RESET is that word: it names the moment, not the child — the play tipped, so we reset the play. Nobody is the villain of a reset.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: the noticing is a SKILL (spotting the wobble before the crash — the raised hand, the too-loud voice); the pause includes the grown-up (everyone freezes — that is the fun and the fairness); and reset means FRESH — the last thirty seconds are not brought to the new start as evidence.

Why this matters

This card is the emergency word for the whole family system: siblings’ games, parent-child standoffs, the pre-dinner spiral. One word, four steps, blame-free — the single highest-leverage habit in the class.

What it teaches

Early warning detection (noticing escalation before it lands), group co-regulation (the shared pause), fresh-start thinking (separating the moment from the child), and family culture — the rituals that make a household feel safe.

Words to learn

noticepausebreatheresetfresh startdo-overtogether

Say this to your child

“"Our family has a magic word: RESET. Here is how it works. Someone NOTICES — a hand goes up — uh oh, this is tipping over. Everyone PAUSEs — mid-motion, even grown-ups, even the dog if he will cooperate. One slow BREATHE together — in through the nose, out slow, the whole room settles an inch. And then: RESET — the game, the moment, the whole bit starts again from the top, fresh. Here is the rule that makes it magic: nobody is in trouble at a reset. Not you, not me. The moment just begins again. Watch me do it to myself sometime — grown-ups need the reset button most of all."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The reset button — for moments going sideways."
  2. Read the panels: the hand-raised girl NOTICEs, the still boy PAUSEs, the folded-hands boy BREATHEs, the refreshed girl RESETs with a small fist.
  3. Play reset-tag below until the word itself does the work.
  4. Demo a grown-up reset: mid-fluster (spilled juice, lost keys), call RESET on yourself — hand up, freeze, one breath, "okay — fresh start." The self-reset is the strongest model in the house.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "nobody is in trouble at a reset — the moment just begins again."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels run the reset: Notice, an attentive girl with her hand raised; Pause, a still boy with closed eyes; Breathe, a boy with folded hands mid-breath; and Reset, a refreshed girl with a small fist up — the family’s emergency word, drawn calm.

Ask your child

"What does the raised hand mean?" "Who has to pause — just kids, or everyone?" "Is anyone in trouble at a reset?" "What gets to start again?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "RESET!" (hand up, delighted) "you have to pause TOO, Daddy" or the merciful one: "we reset, nobody is in trouble."

Out in the real world

Reset moments repeat daily: the game that turns shouty, the dinner-table wobbles, the getting-out-the-door chaos, the sibling spiral. The word works on everyone’s moments — and the day your child calls RESET on YOUR fluster, the habit is fully installed (it will happen; be ready to honour it instantly).

Try it together

Reset Tag: play any fast game — catch, tickle-monster, dance — with the family rule that anyone may shout RESET. When it is called: freeze, one breath together, then the game restarts from the top. The giggles come from the pausing mid-pounce (especially the grown-up caught mid-tickle). After a week of play-resets, the word starts working on real storms — same freeze, same breath, same fresh start, now with a purpose.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who can call reset? What happens to the last thirty seconds? Is anyone in trouble?" Anyone, left behind, nobody — three answers and the family has its button.

Parent tips

Honour every reset instantly — a reset that gets argued with ("we are NOT resetting, we are LEAVING") teaches the word is decoration. And keep the no-blame rule sacred: the moment anyone adds "this is your fault" to a reset, the magic dies. The fresh start IS the discipline; it needs nothing else attached.

This lesson pairs with the Notice, Pause, Breathe & Reset flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Care, Support, Encourage & Comfort — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is for the days someone in the family is having a hard one: four helping words, each one a different way to be there — and a game that puts your child in the comforter’s seat.

What is this?

Care notices the hard time, support carries part of the load, encourage cheers the next try and comfort sits close — a hug, a blanket, a presence, no fixing required.

What does it mean?

Children are usually on the receiving end of these four words — flipping the roles is the lesson: a child invited to care for a struggling grown-up (lightly, kindly, for real) builds empathy faster than any lecture could install it.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: care starts with NOTICING (the sad face, the quiet voice — eyes first); support means carrying a CORNER of the load, not the whole thing (a cup fetched, a sock matched); and comfort does not fix — it sits with. Sitting with is a skill and it is enough.

Why this matters

This card completes the empathy arc that started with notice-understand-comfort-encourage earlier in the class — now the four helping words get deployed on real family days, including the grown-ups’ hard ones.

What it teaches

Nurturing behaviour (the prototype of caregiving), empathy in deployment (noticing, then acting), appropriate helping (matching the help to the need), and emotional reciprocity — the family as a two-way care system.

Words to learn

caresupportencouragecomforthard dayhelpsit with

Say this to your child

“"When someone is having a hard day, there are four helping words. Care — you NOTICE: your face looks sad; care starts with the eyes, always. Support — you CARRY a corner: I will hold the heavy end, I will fetch your cup, I will help look for the keys. Encourage — you CHEER the next try: you have got this; try once more — I am right here. And comfort — you SIT: a hug, a blanket, your shoulder; comfort does not fix the problem and does not have to. Sitting close IS the fix, mostly. Four words. You already have all of them in you — today we take them out and use them."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The four helping words — for someone’s hard day."
  2. Read the panels: the heart-hugging girl CAREs, the hand-on-chest boy SUPPORTs, the fist-up boy ENCOURAGEs, the teddy-hugging girl COMFORTs.
  3. Sort the helps: "Dad lost his keys — care, support, encourage or comfort?" (care: notice. support: help look. encourage: you will find them! comfort: sit with the grumble.) Any order works — the sorting is the thinking.
  4. Play care-for-the-caregiver below: the grown-up has a (mildly, safely theatrical) hard day and the child runs all four.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "comfort does not fix — comfort SITS. Sitting is enough."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the helping words: Care, a girl hugging a pink heart; Support, a boy with a hand on his chest, ready to help; Encourage, a boy cheering with a fist up; and Comfort, a girl hugging her teddy bear — the helping set drawn at teddy-and-family scale.

Ask your child

"Which helping word starts with the eyes?" "What does support carry — the whole load or a corner?" "Does comfort have to fix?" "Who comforted YOU recently?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I noticed you look tired!" (care, live) "I will help carry that!" or the tender one: "come here, I will sit with you."

Out in the real world

Hard days visit every family member: the work wobble, the bad-night’s tiredness, the stubbed toe, the sad news from grandma. Let your child run the four on small scale — a cup fetched, a drawing delivered, a sit-together on the sofa — and debrief gently: "your care helped. That is a real thing you did."

Try it together

Care for the Caregiver: announce (honestly but lightly) that you are having a Hard Five Minutes — and your child is on care duty. Their job: run all four words. They will notice (you look tired), support (fetch the cushion), encourage (you can do the dishes — I mean, you have got this!) and comfort (the blanket, the pat, the sit-together). Accept every offering with full ceremony. Then swap: what helped MOST? The answer teaches you both.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which word starts with noticing? What does support carry? What does comfort do instead of fixing?" Care, a corner, sits with you — three answers and the helping words are on duty.

Parent tips

Accept the child’s comfort without trimming it — the offered half-flat cushion and the pat-pat-pat are exactly as healing as they feel to give; resist redirecting toward "proper" help. And keep the theatrical hard-day SMALL and safe: children comfort best when the storm is clearly survivable — the goal is their competence, not their worry.

This lesson pairs with the Care, Support, Encourage & Comfort flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Listen, Understand, Respond & Forgive — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson upgrades the family’s conversations with four words in the right order: ears to the end, the say-back to prove it, the careful answer and the mend that is always ready.

What is this?

Listen runs to the end of the sentence, understand says back what it heard, respond answers with care and forgive keeps the mend on the shelf, ready for whenever the conversation wobbles.

What does it mean?
